Hon. J. H. KING (Acting Minister of Labour) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting old age pensions, and to provide,-
1.	That the Governor in Council mjty make an agreement with the Lieutenant-Governor in Council of any province for the payment to such province quarterly of an amount equal to one-half of the net sum paid out during the preceding quarter by such province for pensions pursuant to a provincial statute authorizing and providing for the payment of such pensions to the persons and under the conditions hereinafter specified and regulations made under the proposed legislation.
2.	That every agreement so made shall continue in force so long as the provincial statute remains in operation or until after the expiration of ten years from the date upon which notice of an intention to determine the agreement is given by the Governor General to the Lieutenant-Governor of the province with which the same was made.
3.	That before any agreement so made comes into operation, the Governor in Council shall approve the scheme for the administration of pensions proposed to be adopted by the province, and no change in such scheme shall be made by the province without the consent of the Governor in Council.
4.	That all sums payable to any province in pursuance of any such agreement shall be payable from time to time on the certificate of the Treasury board out of any moneys belonging to the consolidated revenue fund of Canada not otherwise appropriated, and the Governor in Council may borrow from time to time such sums as may be required for the purpose of making such payments.
Old Age Pensions
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution you have just read does not contain any new principle. The principle of old age pensions has been recognized in practically all the European countries, in Great Britain, in several of the countries of South America, in several otf the states of the United States of America, and in the Dominions of Australia and New Zealand. In some form or other this principle has been recognized, but it varies according to the desire of the country in which the legislation has been enacted. In some states or some countries the systetm is a contributing one, the individual contributing a sum towards his pension in old age, and the state furnishing another portion. In Great Britain the dual system prevails. There the act was amended

in 1925 to permit of the operation of contributing and non-contributing systems. In the Dominions of Australia and New Zealand the system in force is a non-contributing one.
As I say, the subject is not a new one in Oanada. We find that in 1906-07 a resolution was brought into the House of Commons and adopted. At that time it was set out that it was desirable in the interests of the people of Canada that some provision should be made for old age. In 1911-12 and 191314 the subject was again under discussion, resolutions being introduced into the House. In 1914 a resolution in favour of the adoption of the old age pension system was moved in the House, but the debate was not concluded. In 1922 the House of Comimons adopted a resolution favouring old age pensions. In 1924 a special committee of parliament was appointed to consider the subject, and spent some time delving into the history of old age pensions. It finally recommended to parliament that some system should be adopted in Canada. The recommendations of that committee were as follows:
That an old age pension system be established at ine earliest possible date for deserving indigent persons of seventy years of age and upwards.
That applicants for a pension must be British subjects of at least twenty years residence in Canada, or naturalized subjects df at Oeast (fifteen years' naturalization and twenty-five years residence.
That the maximum rate of pension be $20 per month, which would be lessened by private income or partial ability to earn; that one-half the amount
o.f pension payable be borne by the federal government; the other half, by the provincial government of such provinces as express by legislation their desire to adopt the system-the cost of administration to be borne by the provincial governments.
It will be noted the resolution follows very closely the report of the special committee of 1924. It was suggested the other day by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) that it would be desirable that the House should learn what this scheme would cost tihe nation. I did not understand altogether the right hon. gentleman's reference of a few days ago to this matter. He said at that time:
It is not customary to debate matters upon motion to proceed into committee on a subsequent day. but as these matters of immense consequence, perhaps the government could at least give this modicum of information. I should like if the government could give us an estimate of what the resolutions on the order paper just read will cost the revenue of Canada.
I do not expect a dose estimate at all, but say within a hundred million dollars.
I am satisfied that the right hon. leader of the opposition is not serious in that statement because he has in his possession the re-

ports of the committee on old age (pensions and I have no doubt has familiarized himself with its recommendations. On page 4 of that report the comimittee expresses itself as follows:
Your committee has estimated that under such a system there would be approximately 98,841 eligible pensioners, and if all these were to receive the maximum rate of pension, namely, $20 a month, the federal government's portion of the total yearly expenditure would amount to $11,860,920. This amount, inowever would be reduced by any private income or partial earnings.
So there is no suggestion of an expenditure of $100,000,000.

The question
did not refer to that matter, it referred to all the resolutions on the order paper. What is the use of talking about something that never was said?

I beg my hon.
friend's pardon. I took the statement from Hansard.

My hon. friend
does not follow his own reading. The right hon. leader of the opposition was referring to all the resolutions.
I have taken my own meaning from what the right hon. gentleman said.

And as usual it
is wrong.

The statement
was made to mislead this House. However, I will proceed.
I would.

There is a suggestion in the right hon. gentleman's statement that as a result of the government entering into a scheme of this kind further burdens will be saddled on the Canadian people. That is really not so. There will be no loss financially to the Canadian people. The work of caring for the aged is being done to-day through other channels. The municipal governments and the provincial governments, charitable and other associations are doing that work. I believe under this bill there will be great benefit to those people who find themselves, iir their old age, without sufficient means for their maintenance. There are many people in this country and in all countries, who, through the course of their lives, in some cases not due to their own fault, and in other cases due to their own fault, have been improvident and have not saved up for the rainy day. Anyone who has
been associated with pioneering throughout Canada will realize that there are men who were pioneers for years in this country, and although they have failed to provide for their old age, yet through their efforts and their labours have contributed much to the prosperity of those by whom they were employed.
The proposal to make a federal grant in conjunction with the provinces does not involve the introduction of any new principle, as is well understood in this House. Between the years 1917 and 1920, I think, the government of that day brought down legislation whereby $20,000,000 was set aside to be devoted to the expenditure on roads throughout the Dominion of Canada, known as the national government's contribution to the good roads policy. That principle was accepted; it also has been accepted in the matter of technical schools. Wc enter the provincial field when every year we vote money in aid of agriculture, and it has been accepted as good policy. The central idea of this bill is the establishment of an old age pension scheme under which the Dominion and- such provinces as come into the scheme will each bear one-half of the pensions payable, any administrative expenses to be met by the several provinces concerned. It is expected that the administration will be entrusted to existing provincial organizations such as workmen's compensation boards, and that the administrative expense will thus be very small.

The minister says this is
a scheme to be entered into with the different provinces, but since he has read the report he knows that last year the provinces spoke practically unanimously against it. Has the minister any other reply from the provinces since which would indicate that they had changed their mind?

We had a reply
from the province of British Columbia, which passed a resolution asking for it. The committee did communicate with the various provincial governments, and we have replies from those governments, but apparently the provincial governments to date have not given serious consideration to the old age pension question. The reply from the Premier of Ontario is dated 24th November, 1924, and contains this statement:
I should be glad to consider the matter.
The Manitoba government state that they will be glad to consider the matter with the Premier and the Minister of Public Welfare. The Saskatchewan government wrote that they could see great complications and difficulties in the way. There was no refusal on
mo

the part of provincial governments to enter into the scheme.

No.

I have not seen
them.
In his reply he states absolutely that there is no necessity for a measure of this character.

The proposed bill would not compel any province to enter into the scheme; it is entirely optional with them whether they go into it or not. I have no doubt that when the bill becomes law the advantages to the various provinces will become so apparent that the proposition will be generally accepted throughout Canada.
In order to ensure that provinces which come into the scheme shall be able to rely upon the continuance of the federal grant, it is proposed that this should depend upon an agreement between the Dominion and each of the several provinces, the agreement to be terminable only upon the repeal of the provincial legislation authorizing the payment of pensions, or upon ten years' notice by the Dominion. Upon notice being given, the province may cease granting fresh pensions and will thus find itself at the end of the term of the notice free from liability, except in respect of such negligible number of pensioners as may have continued to receive pensions for at least ten years.
It is considered desirable that the scheme should be indentical in all the provinces and the bill, therefore, specifies the classes of persons who will be entitled to pension. They must be British subjects of 70 years of age and upwards who have been resident in Canada for at least twenty-years before making application, and who have lived in the province in which the application is made for at least five years.
The maximum amount of any pension is to be $240 a year, and from this is to be deducted any income receivable by the pensioner in excess of $125, the upward limit of any pensioner's income, including pension, being thus $365 a year, or $1 a day. No one is pensionable who makes a voluntary transfer of property in order to qualify for pension, but the dwelling house in which the pensioner resides may be transferred to the pension authority, in which case its annual

value is not to be counted as income. Any excess payment of pension on this account is, however, to be recoverable out of the sale of the house by the pension authority when the pensioner ceases to live in it. Provision is also made for the recovery of all pension payments when a pensioner's estate at his death goes to someone who, during his life, has not made a regular and reasonable contribution to his support.
Where, although the pensioner has resided in Canada for twenty years, his residence has been partly in one province and partly in another, the several provinces of residence which have come into the scheme are to contribute to the pension in proportion to the length of the pensioner's residence in each. If he has lived for part of the time in a province which has not come into the scheme, the total pension which would otherwise be payable is to be proportionately reduced.
The bill contains the general principles governing the scheme and provision is made for details as to evidence, method of payment, reports and other like matters being covered by regulation. These, before they are put into force, it is proposed to discuss with the province desirous of making agreements with the Dominion in accordance with the act.

Is there any discrimination
so far as the naturalized citizens of Canada are concerned, as compared with the native born? It was referred to in the report of the committee last year.

No there is no
discrimination under the bill. The committee's report required twenty-five years' residence. I believe this legislation will be of advantage to the people of Canada and will render service to a class of people whom we will always have in our midst and whom we must, from the human point of view, at least provide for in some way, and under this scheme there will be a central authority and one universal scheme that will operate throughout Canada, I believe, to the advantage of this system of taking care of our old people.

I do not rise with the purpose of quarrelling at all with the general policy that this country ought to look after the people who should be looked after. I am not at all sure that they are going to be very much better looked after, however, or that we are going to make very much progress by the adoption of this resolution or the statute that will follow it. In view of the statements of the minister on the other hand, it would seem to me that this is another way of stalling the situation.

Old Age Pensions
We have had nothing further from the provinces. We know where the provinces stand. Now, in the first instance, the minister refers to a query from my right hon. leader as to the cost of governmental legislation as introduced and covered by the resolutions of that day. They covered many things. They were all financial resolutions, and did not have reference merely to this bill.

I had just moved the resolution which was on the order paper and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) said:
I should like if the government could give us an estimate of what the resolutions on the order paper just read will cost the revenue of Canada. I do not ex-pect a close estimate at all, but say within a hundred million dollars.

The whole of
the resolutions read that afternoon.

I had just read
my resolution.

There is no
doubt as to what is meant. The hon. gentleman is surely not so hard up for an argument in favour of his bill as to try to twist a statement like that. Despite what my hon. friend has said in connection with his argument, there may be more merit underlying this proposition than his argument would lead us to believe there is. I am not at all certain that it is a good thing for this parliament to try to look after other business than its own, to try to look after provincial business, when I do not think the most enthusiastic supporters of this government can say it is looking after, as they should be looked after, matters of pressing Dominion importance. This is entirely a provincial matter.
My hon. friend was quite right in saying that during the period after the war Dominion assistance was given to the provinces; that in connection with roads and housing the Dominion government gave the provinces aid. I admit that was done; but I wonder if my hon. friend does not think the objections which were then made, the force of which was admitted but brushed temporarily to one side owing to the financial position the country found itself in, were not really right and that is that the power of taxation resting in the Dominion, and in the right of the Dominion, should not be exercised in ease of the provinces which, under the British North America Act, have the right of taxation for provincial purposes. The point is rather a serious one. The hon. member did not refer only to roads and housing which, as he knows perfectly well, were matters of emergency having to do with provincial fin-14011-123
ances at that time and a pressing necessity, not only for the purpose of aiding these works but much more so for the purpose of providing labour to the unemployed and also for the purpose of looking after the shortage in houses, something which otherwise could not and would not have been done. Agriculture is a Dominion interest	just	as	much as it is	a provincialinterest.	It	is	a Dominion child, a Dominion care, just as much as it is a provincial care. There	we	are on common	ground, butI point	out	to	my hon. friend	that we are

This matter is not new; it is old, as my hon. friend says. The government during the four years of its existence played with it; they passed it on from time to time. We had committees and committees; we had reports; we even had reports adopted, but nothing was done. Why? The sole reason nothing was done was that none of the provinces wanted it 'and to-day none of the provinces, with the exception of possibly one, want it. My hon. friend thinks he can vouch for that one, namely, his own province of British Columbia.
I want to refer the House to the material it has before it just to show how this matter was really gone into for the purpose of seeing whether the provinces wanted it or not, and then I am going to consider very shortly why the provinces would not want it. Hon. members will find at page 455 of volume 62 of the Journals of the House of 1925 a report by the special committee appointed to inquire into an old age pension system for Canada as to the stand of the provinces. I think I had better read the report. It states:
Your committee has given careful consideration to the aforesaid correspondence, and also to the correspondence more recently received from premiers and ministers of several provinces. Briefly, the views of the several provincial governments are as follows:
1.	New Brunswick.-Under date of May 23, 1925, the Premier (Hon. Mr. Veniot) writes:	"This province is
now considering the establishment of what As known as widows' pension, and we are not prepared to take any decision in the matter of an old age pension. While I do not disapprove of the old age pension, and feel that it would be a good thing, yet it would be impossible for me to commit the province to any action in this matter at the present moment."
That is the stand of New Brunswick and the minister tells us that nothing has been heard from that province since then.

Old Age Pensions

2.	Quebec.-Under date of February 17, 1925, the
Minister of Public Works and Labour (Hon. Mr. Galipeault) writes:	"On the occasion of the recent
visit of the delegates of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, this question was taken up and, although it was not submitted in the regular way to the cabinet, I understood from the remarks of my colleagues that it could be no question for the province of Quebec, considering the obligations actually imposed upon it, of adopting a law which would take care of the old age pensions in this province."
We there have a definite refusal and the press of this week confirms again that refusal.
Will the hon. member repeat that because I could not catch it?

I just paused to point out that in the correspondence which the leader of the Progressive party will find at page 455 of volume 62 of the Journals of the House of Commons, Quebec gave a direct negative to the proposal and that direct negative of Quebec then given by the Minister of Public Works and Labour of that province is confirmed by the premier of the province himself only this week.
3.	Nova Scotia.-Under date of June 2, 1925, the
Premier (Hon. Mr. Armstrong) writes:	"In view of
the importance of the 6ubject-matter, and the lack of an opportunity to fully consider the same, I was instructed to advise you that (without a further and better understanding of the subject-matter and without an opportunity to fully discuss it with your committee, no action would be taken upon the matter at present."
No action has yet been taken. There was time and opportunity for a better understanding, but this government in its haste to introduce this legislation for a very obvious reason which has been explained in the House more than once, has not taken up the question again with the province which thus writes and has heard nothing further from it since.
4.	Prince Edward Island.-Under date of May 22,
1925, the Premier (Hon. Mr. Stewart) writes:	"In
this province, as you probably are aware, except in the towns, we have no municipal government, consequently all assistance to indigent and aged persons is furnished directly 'by the provincial government, either in the provincial infirmary or 'by monthly contributions to private persons who become responsible for their support. I have read over your letter and the accompanying report with interest. I shall place the matter before my government at its next meeting and will then advise you of its decision."
No decision has yet been made, nor has there been any further exchange of correspondence such as might have made it easy to get some real progress in the matter. Furthermore, the difficulty of the provinces in dealing with the proposal is amply illustrated by that letter. The province has its own machinery for looking after the aged and the indigent, and it takes care of them either in private institutions or by means of donations or payments to families who will take

the needy in and care for them. What will the provinces do with all that machinery? Are they going to scrap their own machinery? I do not know how the provincial organizations have worked out but I should have thought certainly that this was a question for the people of the provinces themselves to settle one way or the other. I am at a loss to know what is to become of all these various provincial institutions throughout the country. There is some provision in the matter of relief to the aged and indigent in nearly all the provinces, and I believe there are a few provinces that have not recognized their obligation in this regard. But generally speaking, either through the municipality or through the province as a whole, they have at least taken some steps in the direction of earing for those who are in destitute circumstances within their territories.
Now I come to Ontario. The letter received from that province is quite brief. Under date November 24, 1924, the Premier writes:
I shall be glad to consider the matter.
And there it stands. On behalf of the province of Manitoba the Attorney General there writes under date February 25, 1925:
We are in the midst of our session just now with a multiplicity of matters requiring immediate disposition. I shall, however, take the matter up *with the Premier and the Minister of Public Welfare at the earliest opportunity.
And this government, although that session was concluded months ago, have not done a thing in the way of considering the question with the authorities of Manitoba. Again, the matter rests in abeyance. As regards Saskatchewan, the Hon. Mr. Gardiner, the present Premier of that province, writes on November 19, 1924:
The government of Saskatchewan is of opinion that an old age pension scheme for Canada can be best adopted by the federal government alone.
There we have a new light on the subject. A new idea is given us, but of course it is opposed to the principle of this scheme. That idea is that instead of a fifty per cent division as the minister proposes, the Dominion government should meet the whole cost. The letter proceeds:
There would seem to be so much difficulty in the way of providing any scheme that would 'be suitable to all the nine provinces of Canada as to make it almost impossible, and it will be readily understood that if any number of the provinces were to remain out, it would be almost impossible to adopt any scheme which would not subject those provinces within the arrangement to considerable expense that should rightfully be borne by those outside the scheme. While we are disposed to think that an old age pension scheme should be undertaken, the difficulties in the way of the suggested scheme appear almost, if not entirely, insurmountable.

That is what the great province of Saskatchewan says in connection with this proposal, and in connection with the report upon which this bill is drawn up. The objections of that province to the scheme
4 p.m. are summed up in the opinion that the difficulties are insurmountable. Apparently they have the idea in Saskatchewan that there are real differences between the various provinces, that there is a separate problem to be faced in relation to each province in the matter of relief, and that therefore it is almost if not entirely impossible to devise a method that would be suitable to the whole Dominion, owing to the great diversity that exists in the conditions throughout the country. My hon. friend has put his finger on the crux of the whole question. What is behind that question of his? What is it that gives merit and weight to it? The whole thing is provincial and my hon. friend's point is well taken. No contributory scheme, no insurance, nor anything of that kind could be worked out through the agency of the Dominion. State responsibility in the matter of the proper maintenance of aged citizens has been recognized-.

Referring to your letter of the 12th instant, asking to be advised with regard to the authority of parliament to legislate on the subject of old age pensions, I may say that this subject does not fall specifically within any of the enumerated subjects given to the Dominion under section 91 of the British North America Act, but does in my judgment fall within the subject "Property and Civil Rights in the Province" committed to the provinces under section 92. I am of opinion, therefore, that the subject matter of pensions has been entrusted to the provincial legislatures rather than to parliament. I do not mean to suggest that parliament has not the power to legislate upon the subject so as to assist the provinces or to establish an independent voluntary scheme, provided that in either case the legislation does not trench upon the subject matter of property and civil rights in the provmce.

I think we have to take that fact into consideration. Reference has been made to the attitude of the different provinces, and I followed carefully the remarks of the last speaker on that point. Considering the answers of provincial governments on the whole

you might regard their language as favourable. I noticed that a resolution with respect to old age pensions was introduced in the Manitoba legislature, which is now sitting, and one of the speakers declared the matter was one for the Dominion parliament to deal with; he appeared to think that it could better be dealt with by the federal authority. I am therefore inclined to believe that the province of Manitoba is in favour of Dominion legislation in regard to old age pensions. The province of Saskatchewan is in favour of the Dominion taking this matter up. So is the province of Alberta. The provinces of Ontario, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia have not had anything to say in opposition to legislation by the Dominion on the question.
It may be asked, "Why enter into any more commitments when taxation bears so heavily upon the people at the present time?" The question is a pertinent one. Everyone recognizes that Canada is a heavily taxed country. Coming from the province of Manitoba I may say that there the legislation along this line is as advanced as in any other province of the Dominion. I recognize, however, that it is possible to travel too fast, and that it is possible to pay too high a p'rice for something that may be very desirable. At the same time I am not prepared to admit that an old age pension system is going to increase the burdens of the people or to add to taxation to any extent. A great many people in this country are taken care of in other ways thaq by an old age pension. There is a large class of the people whose circumstances place them far beyond the possibility of want or of requiring public assistance of any kind. There are also civil servants and employees in public institutions and corporations who are taken care of by pensions in their old age after a certain number of years of service. But the present resolution deals with an entirely different class of our population, and it is a class with whom I have a great deal of sympathy -I refer to the ordinary people, the common labourer if you please, the man who works for a day's wage and finds it difficult to provide for the daily necessities o'f his family and himself much less to lay by anything for his declining years. This man has rendered a service to his country, he has well earned the pension that may be coming to him in his old age; and although the providing of pensions may press somewhat heavily upon our people I cannot help feeling that those who pay the taxes are quite willing to do something for those poor unfortunates who do not earn sufficient to lay by anything for a
rainy day. So I am quite prepared to consider this matter seriously, and see if we cannot evolve legislation that will meet the situation. In any case these people have to be taken care of. The last speaker wondered what we were going to do with some of the public institutions that we already maintain.
I do not know whether my hon. friend is aware of the fact that this legislation, if it goes into effect, will only take care of a certain section of our population, those who have been twenty years in the Dominion. There are other requirements which have to be met before pensions can be granted so that a numerous section of the Canadian population will be unable to take advantage of the provisions of any act we may pass. Erom some little experience I have had in connection with ihe administration of certain public charities in the city of Winnipeg, and I have already mentioned this fact in the House, I am inclined to believe, there are people in receipt of what is called charity who should not be reduced to that necessity. As I have already said, they have given sufficient service to the country to entitle them to financial assistance to meet the necessities of their old age, and the aid so granted should not be regarded in any way as charity. I should like to see the spirit of thrift inculcated amongst our people so as to try and ensure that they will not at'any time be in the position to need public aid. I can look back to my boyhood days in the Old Land beyond the seas, and I can remember how abhorrent the idea oi charity was to the people there. I remember, and I allude to it with pride, the sturdy honesty and independence so characteristic of the Scottish people. So marked was this characteristic that they would have to be very hard up before they would accept anything in the nature of charity. I do not want the old age pension to be considered in that light. I would rather have it regarded as something which the people receiving it earned during the long years in which they toiled for a living.

taking better care of our old people, to prevent them being stigmatized as paupers after they reach the age of seventy. The time has come when old, wom-out industrial workers who are not able to earn over $240 a year, ought not to be stigmatized as paupers or placed in poorhouses. I was in the Old Country last summer and had an opportunity to witness the beneficial results of a scheme of this kind. It is true the municipalities and the provinces have at the present time facilities for taking care of old people, but in discussing a bill of this nature, designed to provide for our worthy pioneers, we ought not to give much consideration to the question of preserving old, worn-out poor-houses made of brick and mortar.
Another point I want to make is that the cost of this scheme, whether you call it $11,000,000 or $23,000,000, has been arrived at after taking into consideration the number of people who will be eligible to share in its benefits. In my opinion this government is entitled to great credit for introducing this measure and making provision of which the provinces can avail themselves. I think, Mr. Speaker, that all who have in any way represented workmen whether politically or industrially will agree that one of the greatest fears among the working class is that of not being able to provide for old age, not being able to earn sufficient wages to ensure that in the evening of life they will not be stigmatized as paupers. This fear has a very unsettling effect which this legislation will very largely
remove. I do not agree, of course, that the amount of the pension is sufficient, but the measure is a step in the right direction.

Public opinion is advancing very quickly along these lines. Mr. Speaker, I desire very briefly to record my objections to the resolution now before the House. Personally, I am disposed to agree with the view of the hon. member for Bran-

don (Mr. Forke) that this question should be treated as a non-partisan one. It affects all classes. It has never been to my knowledge the subject of a debate upon the platforms of this country. My objections to the resolution are threefold. First, I think it is a mistake that Canada should, by such a measure as this, advertise to the world that our country affords [DOT]so slight and narrow a margin between income and living that when many people reach the age of seventy years it becomes necessary for the state to step in and maintain them. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) referred to the matter of the dole in England. Surely the dole in England and the proposed old age pension scheme in Canada do not make for thrift on the part of the people. On the contrary I contend that the effect will be to destroy thrift. Again, the amount of expenditure involved is no slight matter. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) placed at approximately $12,000,000 the charge upon the revenues of the Dominion, and if the scheme is carried out a charge of some $24,000,000 is involved when the burden upon the provinces is added. Surely an additional annual expenditure of $24,000,000 is not a matter to be lightly considered by a people so heavily taxed as we in Canada are to-day.
I do not know, I cannot tell whether or not the government is serious in this proposal. There is no doubt that the proposal is at present at least utterly impracticable. You cannot pass and enforce legislation of this character until you have the consent and co-operation of every province in Canada without doing a grave and serious injustice to the taxpayer. As to the attitude of Quebec there is no secret. Only on Tuesday of this week the premier of that province, Mr. Taschereau, stated in no uncertain terms that he and his government-and he did not speak as an individual; he spoke for his government, using the plural-that the province of Quebec wants none of this legislation. It had had enough, he said, of legislation of this character from the parliament of Canada in recent years, legislation such as housing assistance, grants for the extension of roads and so on, all of which I personally opposed, although that may be of little consequence, but which grants in their operation have involved serious charges upon the coun-

try without adequate compensation to the people. Let me read the words of the Hon. Mr. Taschereau. He said:
If Ottawa wishes to come to the aid of our farmers, and of our old people, the matter is for them, but I think that the matter should rest with Ottawa, for we are not prepared to go into a system of partnership. If there devolves upon us the need of caring for our old people, and for our farmers in the matter of credits, we will do the best we can under the circumstances, but as to embarking once more upon a system similar to that as to housing, we are not prepared to go.
How would this scheme work out? If this government or this parliament is determined to proceed to put into operation an old age pension scheme, in order to be equitable it must provide a pension of $120 a year for every individual indigent person of seventy years of age and permit the province to supplement that grant by an equal amount, making the $240 referred to in the resolution. Otherwise what happens? Suppose eight of the nine provinces accept this scheme, contributing their $120, and Quebec refuses to join, as it has already refused through the mouth of its premier only this week. The residents of that province would be obliged- the logic is irresistible-to contribute their quota towards the moneys that would be paid to old age pensioners in the 5 p.m. other provinces of Canada. In my opinion that one fact, which is indisputable, is enough to condemn the measure and to warrant the government in withdrawing it until it shall have received more mature consideration, or until all of the provinces without exception are willing to join hands and parliament resolves that, under those circumstances, the legislation is such as should be proceeded with.

Mr. Speaker, I deem it my duty to take part in this debate; however, I shall foe brief. I must admit that I am somewhat astonished at the attitude taken by a number of our opponents, seeing that this question has already been thoroughly considered 'without any reference to party spirit. The hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White) has just stated that he is not in favour of such a scheme. Indeed, his statement astonishes me, especially when I see his friends on your left, Sir, and himself rise to oppose this resolution,. As far as I am concerned, it is with a deep feeling of satisfaction, I would even add of pride, that I give my support to this measure which will provide a pension for old age.
I see in this resolution the realization of a project which I have cherished throughout my life. Indeed, in the course of the session

Old Age Pensions
of 1922, I had the honour to move in the House a resolution which read as follows: "That, in the opinion of the House, the Dominion government should1 consider the advisability of devising ways and means for the establishment of a system of old age pensions in Canada." This resolution was unanimously carried at the time. However, it was only in the course of the session of 1924 that the government appointed a special committee, of which I had the honour to be a member, in order to study this pension scheme. This committee in its report to the House, recommended that a pension of twenty dollars per month be paid to every citizen who, having reached the age of seventy, was without any income, providing he was a British subject. Considering that the sum involved to meet the payments of this pension might amount to more than $20,000,000 per year, the committee suggested to the government, owing to the depressed financial conditions of the country, that half of said expenditure should be paid 'by the provincial governments. I notice that the present bill is based on said report. I am pleased to see it and I wish to congratulate the government.
I especially wish to thank the Prime Minister who has always shown himself favourable to this project and always listened to me sympathetically each time I broached the subject to him. Moreover, Sir, as I stated when I moved my resolution in the House, in 1922, it behooves the Liberal party, the people's party in opposition to the large interests, to have such a philanthropic and humane measure adopted. The fact is so true that at the time of the Liberal convention, held in Ottawa, in August, 1919, at the time of our party's important convention, a special motion having such an aim in view was moved and! adopted. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, himself, at a large meeting held in Montreal, in 1916, stated that as soon as the war would be over, one of the paramount problems :n this country would be the establishment of pensions for old age, and with this aim in view, he said, that he had confided to his principal lieutenants the care of studying this question.
After all. Mr. Speaker, similar legislation exists in almost every country. As early as 1908 the British parliament adopted an old age pension scheme. In France, Germany, Denmark, New Zealand, everywhere, there are old age pensions. Do you not think then that the time has arrived when, in Canada, we should do something for those old citizens, those old servants who have contributed largely to the progress and development of the country, who have worked during thirty, forty and even fifty years to enrich others and have spent their whole capital-as capacity for work, is really the workman's capital-who, moreover, as soon as their strength gives way, worn out by old age and work, are reduced to poverty, become a burden to their children or are forced to take refuge in the poorhouse? I say that it is the duty of the state to come to the assistance of these old people.
Some, perhaps, might remark that these people should have been provident and have practised economy during their youth, but every member in this House knows perfectly well that wages are never sufficiently high to allow of savings, as the wages paid to workmen are always based on the cost of living. The cost of living for a workman's family of five or six children is figured out, anci tne result of this calculation fixes the wages he is to receive.	_	.
How can he possibly economize when he is paid hardly enough to allow the strict necessities to his family? Yet, the workman is entitled as well as the rich man to some comfort in this world, he has a heart, loves his children just like the rich man, and he would like very much to give them greater facilities than he has had in order to face the struggles of life; but how can he realize such a desire with the small wages of two or three dollars per day? I especially made reference to the workmen, because they are the people who will benefit the most by this pension act. However, let it be "well understood that all those who have reached the age of seventy, men and women, if they are in need, whether they have had, during their lifetime, a trade or been in business, will benefit by this pension legislation, providing they have lived like honest citizens. One objection which I have heard against this scheme, Sir, is that it would discourage thrift and personal initiative: the workman would be less thrifty being assured that the state would provide for him in his old age. To my point of view, this objection is not a serious one. If this measure, as some believe, was of a nature to create abuses, the European countries, where this act is in force, would think of abolishing it, but on the contrary, they are improving it from year to year. On that score, the government should abolish the retirement funds of the civil employees; the banks and corporations, where such pension funds exist, should abolish them. Quite the contrary, I think that this pension act would be of a nature to stimulate the energy of workmen who would feel themselves backed by the

state, and immigration, would benefit through it when it was known that Canada looks after its citizens when they are old and feeble.
I will close my remarks, Sir, and I feel firmly convinced that no member of this House would vote against this measure.

Mr. Speaker, I am strongly in favour of the principle of old age pensions. This matter has been before parliament for a number of years. The question which concerns me now is the practicability of the government's
scheme and the sincerity of the government in submitting this question to parliament. The principle of old age pensions has been adopted in a number of countries, including Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand, Belgium, France and Italy. Old age pensions is a form of social legislation, an advancement and progress in social legislation in keeping with advancements which have been going on in other forms of legislation during the past hundred years. One of the most serious objections raised against old age pensions is the charge that it involves a very heavy expense to the state. I believe that that contention is an economic delusion. Our aged people are, in fact, supported by the country, but that support is in the form of charitable institutions, the donations of philanthropic and benevolent people, or assistance provided by the children or relatives of aged people. No one will contend that men and women over seventy years of age, the aged people of this country, do not in fact receive the necessary clothing and food which they require, so that the proposal before parliament is not a question of adding to the expense of our country as an economic entity, but rather a question of the method of distributing responsibility.
The question we have to face is, has civilization advanced to the point where the state should take in its hands the distribution of the maintenance and support of our aged people, or must we leave that duty to the kindness and charity of benevolent people? From a purely economic point of view I would like to hear an answer to the contention that old age pensions is not a charge upon the economic state. That is the first point I wish to make.
I recall vividly each day, leaving my office in Vancouver, seeing a man, seventy-six years old, bent with the toil of half a century and ill from his very indigence, engaged in scrubbing floors and in doing the work of a janitor's helper. It is in the actualities of experience that we obtain judgment and advice on the wisdom of legislation, in many cases, and knowing that this matter was coming before parliament, I questioned this old man. I asked him about his life, how it was that he had nothing to provide for his old age, whether he had a family, how he was getting along and how he faced his work. His story was the story of thousands of men throughout Canada, one of difficulties and illnesses in his early years. He was a temperate man, sober in thought and habits; he worked as he was able to work, but had not been endowed by Providence with the mentality and skill necessary to provide abundantly for himself and he found, at the age of seventy-six years,
Old Age Pensions

that he was practically a pauper; in ill health; broken and bent, and leaning over the floor doing his work as a janitor's helper. He did not know how long he would be able to keep going. The great fear of his life was what was going to happen to him when he reached the point of being unable to longer earn his living.
In this country, as in every country, not because of the conditions of the country but because of the frailty of human nature, there are thousands upon thousands of such people. The report of the special committee tells us that there would be 98,841 people eligible for pensions. It cannot be said, however, that all these people over the age of seventy years would be entitled to pension. A great many have private means; others are supported by their children or by friends, and would not receive a pension. The committee reported that the cost of maintaining this scheme, so far as the federal government is concerned, would be $11,S60,000. I think hon. gentlemen will agree with me that at once we can deduct quite a large amount owing to the fact that many people who are over seventy would not receive the pension. Let us say you reduce this amount to $10,000,000 a year. As I pointed out in the first part of my argument, you are not adding that burden of $10,000,000 a year to Canada as an economic entity. You are merely distributing the obligation throughout the state upon people who are less disposed to be benevolent and less disposed to help the aged and infirm and people entitled to assistance of this kind. That is all you are doing. Now $10,000,000 is approximately one-thirty-fourth of the total revenue of this country, which is in the neighbourhood of $340,000,000 a year. I would prefer to have old age pensions than to have the Hudson Bay railway and many other public expenditures which have been made during the last few years. I would prefer to cut down the public expenditure, apart from the fixed charges. I would prefer to put the aged and infirm in this country in a position of comfort, assured at least of the bare necessities of life, than to make large public expenditures, engage in construction work and a number of other economic activities of doubtful benefit to Canada.

I would ask my hon.
friend to include in that list the Welland canal.

Yes, I would include a great many expenditures that have been made by both governments during many years. But those of which I have particular knowledge are the expenditures made by the present govern-

ment, and among them I omitted to mention $9,000,000 for Quebec harbour. That alone would pay the pension bill for a year.
I think if any hon. member of this chamber were confronted in private with the proposition whether or not this country could afford $10,000,000 for the aged men and women of this country, leaving apart the form in which the assistance should be granted, he would agree to the principle of it; but what I am chiefly concerned in is the government's sincerity, and in making that statement I do not want to be charged with raising the question of party politics. I think this question is one of the most important before the people of Canada. It is far above partisan politics. It is a question, the solution of which will bring more real happiness to the maximum number of people in this country than any other enactment which has been before the House for a great many years, and for that reason I want to keep it out of party politics as much as possible. But in considering the merits of the matter we have to review the conduct of the government in connection with this proposal during the past four years.
When the last parliament opened in 1922 the question of old age pensions was raised by a number of hon. gentlemen in different speeches. My friend Mr. Irvine, from Calgary, took a very active part in those discussions, but during those four years the government did not do a single thing of a constructive nature in the matter of old age pensions, although they were pledged in the most serious and solemn manner by their convention of 1919, by their party platform in 1921, and by the speeches of every important political leader on the government side throughout Canada during the contest of 1921. Everywhere they proclaimed themselves the champions of old age pensions, but when they were in power, although they had sixty-five Progressive members nearly every one of whom was a supporter of old age pension, the government found devious ways and means to avoid bringing down legislation and putting an old age pension scheme into effect. If they found excuses during the four years from 1921 to 1925, when they had sixty-five Progressive members w*ho would support them, and who enabled them to have a majority sometimes as high as 160 or more, what likelihood is there that the government will press this matter to a conclusion now?

Another loophole is contained in paragraph 3. I submit that the law aimed at is a commendable one, and I commend the government for the initial stages they have undertaken in a non-partisan way. il commend them for taking the step, although the experience of the past would indicate that they may not carry it into effect. I think that from the serious business point of view, from the economic aspect, those who think that the giving of a pension is going to add an additional burden to the country are suffering from a delusion. It is adding no burden, it is only distributing an existing burden among those who at present should pay but will not pay. It is only relieving those people who are benevolently and charitably inclined and who will give a great deal of what they earn, while others will give nothing. It is only in the taking and distributing of this burden that the state will interfere by legislation of this character. I hope to see some measure go through. If I find when the bill is introduced that its provisions are reasonable, if the measure shows an indication of sincerity, I for one will support it, because I do not think that partisan politics should be interjected in connection with a bill of such great importance to the nation and one involving such great advancement in its social reforms. We are going to become old. Some of us may require the $20 per month which is to be provided. I hope that I shall not, but I know many will. And when I think of the people whom I have seen in difficulties and in trouble; when I think of the old man who always comes to my mind when this question is discussed; when I think of that man seventy-six years of age there on his bended knees

scrubbing the floors; when I remember the story I have heard of that honest man who has done his life's work faithfully and who has devoted half a century to the struggle for a bare existence; when I think of the benefits which will accrue from the action of the state in providing even $20 a month to enable that man to keep body and soul together; -when I think of the sunshine of happiness that will brighten the evening of his life, my heart, my conscience, my judgment and my resolve spring forth to make possible for the aged of our land a comfort and a joy which no true Canadian citizen, animated by high and benevolent ideas, would deny.

I cannot think of any legislation that has been so long in the hatching as this particular measure. I observe amongst those who supported the resolution the names of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. Maelean of York, the Hon. Mr. Lemieux and Mr. Bourassa. I do not know whether the last-named gentleman is my friend to my right or not. The motion was not pressed to a vote, but was withdrawn. That was a preliminary step. I see that Sir George Foster, amongst others, supported the resolution on that occasion. No report other than a verbal statement made by the chairman was presented to the House. The hon. ex-Minister of Finance read part of a letter from the Hon. John Oliver, of British Columbia, addressed to Mr. Raymond, chairman of the committee. I want to make a slight
allusion to the remarks of the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White), and I do so in a most friendly spirit, realizing as I do that his whole life and environment have been such as to have removed him utterly from the people whose conditions we are considering to-day. The hon. member told us that the act would discourage thrift among the people Well, that idea was prevalent at the time when women wore crinolines, and I think it went out about the same time as the crinolines did. Moreover, it has been proved by the experience of every pension system in the world that such a scheme does not discourage thrift; rather is the contrary the case. We know also that the proposed act provides for a small income which will be allowed, so to speak, outside of the pension, so that there, too, is encouragement for thrift in a small way.
Old Age Pensions

I do not know of any idea that is more difficult to combat than this. The man who has made some measure of success of his own life is very apt to take the attitude that if someone else has not been equally successful, it is due to his own negligence or laziness or to some mental disability. It is hard for a matter of this kind to be discussed quite fairly in a gathering of this kind, composed of gentlemen who for the most part are very much removed from the circumstances of the class of people whom we are considering. Some of us may perhaps have inherited money which by judicious business manipulation we have managed to increase, while others of us have been more or less the architects of our own fortune. At any rate the majority of members of parliament have some means apart from their sessional allowance and are in a greater or smaller degree what is called successful; and they think therefore that they are in no danger of ever falling a prey to the misfortunes of old age and poverty. It was Bunyan, I think, who once said when he saw a man being led to the gallows, "But for the grace of God, there goes John Bunyan." If the most fortunate man amongst us were stripped of the advantages which opportunity and luck and chance, or possibly Providence, has given him there would be little for him to boast about in comparison with others. I never see a down-and-outer on the street bumming the price of a drink without thinking that under less happy circumstances I, too, might have been in his situation.
It is far from being the case that poverty necessarily indicates negligence or laziness or incompetence of anjr kind. Sickness is a misfortune that is apt to befall anyone, and the wage-earner and his family are not immune. I was going to say that ignorance was a disease; at any rate it is a disability for which you cannot blame a man if he has not had training. How often have we seen men who have scraped and saved and denied themselves all their lives in order to have a little income in their old age, and who have lost it in a few hours by being gold-bricked by some smart rascal. It may be said of such a man that he should not have allowed himself to be taken in, but we must remember that he had not the necessary knowledge to protect himself. Occasionally we see widows and others entrusting their money to agents or lawyers who take advantage of them and embezzle their savings. I am not casting a cheap slur on lawyers, for I know that they are reputable people, but they are liable to fall by the wayside like others. I [Mr, N'eiU.1
have known people who were not lawyers who have embezzled money belonging to their relations or their friends. Again, we have known men who have worked hard all their lives, contented, willing, and who apparently possessed every attribute of success, and yet they have fallen down at every turn. It never seemed possible for them to get ahead, although they could not be accused of any particular fault.
Again let us take the case of the woman whose husband has been a waster, a drunkard, a profligate. He has neglected to take care of his wife and family, and they are in a destitute condition. This is one of the objections-I do not say it was the only objection, but it was one of them-that decided the committee against a contributory scheme. The contributory scheme assumes that a man must contribute something before he can get a pension. Then you must also have the other feature; that if he failed to contribute he would not get a pension. Then what are you going to do with a woman? A woman may be everything desirable, but she may marry a man who turns out to be a bad character and who may abandon her with a family to bring up, perhaps by taking in washing. Then when she gets old and unable to work she hears about this pension. She applies for it and is told "No, you cannot have a pension; you can starve or go to the poorhouse, because your husband, between the ages of twenty-five and some other age did not pay his regular contributions." It was to avoid things of that kind and an enormous duplication of such cases that a contributory scheme was decided against. It was also found to be unworkable in several countries, except in very narrow phases.
The hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White) told us in almost awestruck tones that each one of these pensions was going to cost the province $120. Spoken in that way it sounds a lot of money, especially when you are going to give it to someone else, but supposing conditions were reversed; suppose the hon. member or others in this House were to look at the situation from the other end of the telescope. Would the hon. member, or would any of us in our old age, either for ourselves or for our relatives, contemplate with equanimity the possibility of existing on a pension of $240 a year? It has been well said that riches take wings, and that phrase is increasingly true to-day, in the turmoil of modern commercial life. It is also an old saying that it is only three generations from shirt sleeves to shirt sleeves. That does not, of course, seem possible to us, sitting here

I do know that on the committee of which we have been speaking, which drew up this report which the government have largely followed, there were three representatives from the province of Quebec, and they were all unanimous in voting for a report containing these principles.
To go back to the resolution, there may be and, I am sure will be, demands from the people whom it is intended to benefit. They will not be satisfied with the amount suggested, and they will think it should begin at an earlier period. I think possibly some consideration might also be given to the claims of the soldiers, that the pension in their case should begin somewhat earlier than
in the case of a civilian. I would throw out the suggestion that where a man has spent say two years actively engaged in the trenches, he might be entitled to a pension say ten years sooner than the ordinary civilian. That may be a matter for future consideration. I would point out that the bill follows the same custom which prevails in Great Britain, with the pension beginning at the age of seventy. There is in England a provision now, mixed up with some other form of unemployment or sickness insurance, whereby the pension may begin at sixty-five, but that part is contributory; the regular non-contributory pensions begins at the age of seventy.
I was much struck with the evidence of a gentleman who appeared before that committee. He was a railway man, evidently . high in one of the railway organizations, and the attitude he took seemed so appropriate that I would like to repeat it. Speaking on behalf of the railway men he said:	"We
railwaymen do not want your old age pension bill; it is nothing to us. We have organizations of our own that will afford us a pension greater than any you propose to give. Inasmuch as we pay taxes we would be contributing for the benefit of another class of people and rve would derive no benefits ourselves, but as working men we will be pleased to do so." We asked him, as we asked all witnesses, at what age he thought the pension should begin, and what he thought should be the minimum amount. He said, "Gentlemen, I would not pretend to give you advice on either of those points, because the essential feature is to get the principle started. To get that started it may be necessary for you to begin at a scale lower than it should be and at an age later that it should be, and speaking on behalf of the working men we will be satisfied to get the principle established. There will be no danger of its being reduced, and once you have the thing started and find the cost, you will be in a better position to see whether or not you can increase it as the years go by." I was greatly impressed with his remarks, and I think they had a good deal to do with the decision of the committee.

Let me recall, too, that this legislation has been twice endorsed by the parliament of Canada, not in successive years, but in the year 1912, I think it was, and again in 1922. Further on:
The measure, then, as it stand3, is the product of the united wisdom of parliament.
Would to God we could say the same thing! It represents the determination of the whole country to carry out what it has come to look upon as a sacred duty towards a large number of the more defenceless of its citizens.

As to this old age pension, it does not seem to me there can be two ideas about it. It is intended absolutely for a class of people who need support and who, I think, are entitled to it-people who for various reasons have not been able to lay by enough in earlier life to carry them through their old age. I do not suppose there is any class of men that has a better opportunity than my own profession, that of medicine, of seeing the homes in this country and of realizing that there are many people to whom a measure of this kind will be of great assistance. In moving around and meeting all classes of people in very intimate circumstances, we see many who are almost in absolute want, people who are making the bravest struggle they can and putting up a front but to whom a little assistance of this kind will be a great help. There is this about it, and we may as well realize it, that the people who have money are entitled to help out in such a case as this.
There are a great many reasons why people are not able to look after themselves when they get to the age of seventy years. We must understand that the men who are now [DOT] eligible for this pension at seventy years of age were raising their families forty or fifty years ago, when the wages paid were very low and when it was exceedingly difficult for a man to bring up a family and lay by any money. Even to-day we know it is a very difficult matter to lay by the sum of $4,500, which would be the principal required to bring in an income equivalent to the pension, and at the same time to bring up a family and keep a roof over your head. It is easy to say that if these people had been provident and pushing they would have been able to get good jobs. Everybody cannot get good jobs. No matter how much effort they put forth there is always a certain number of people that cannot get good jobs as

foremen or positions of that kind, and we have got to look out for them.
There is another thing that tells against these elderly people at the present time. Manufacturers and other employers of labour do not want elderly men. When men reach the age of fifty-five or sixty their sight and hearing is defective; they are subject to a little shaking of the hands, and it is not considered safe to have them working around machinery-in fact the Workmen's Compensation Act rather discourages employers from engaging them. Consequently the earning days of these people are over when they reach the age mentioned. When that time comes, if they have been able to lay a little money by, they are forced to live on their capital. I do not think it is wise to impose too heavy a burden on the young people of a family. I have often seen cases where young people were held back a great deal by having to shoulder too heavy a burden in the way of looking after the older people. I do not argue that young folks should be relieved from support of their parents or dependents. I do not think that at all; indeed in the province of Ontario there is a law which compels children to support or partly support their parents if they are at all in a position to do so, and I do not think any legislation of the character contemplated here should relieve them of that responsibility. But I do say this: If the young people were relieved in a good many cases just when they are struggling to make a start for themselves it would be a very helpful thing indeed.
This idea of helping old people through the medium of a pension is just a sign of advancing civilization. In the old days when aged people could not keep up with the procession they simply dropped out and died. Then the municipalities and communities began to take them into homes where they spent their declining days. That was a step forward. Then came our houses of refuge. We have one in our own county, and from my personal knowledge I can say that it is a well conducted institution. I
am not sure that I can add anything of value to the discussion, but I desire to take advantage of the opportunity to state my sympathy with the principle of the resolution. I have always felt that when men and women who have spent a lifetime of labour, perhaps rearing families and aiding in the production of the country, thus adding to the national prosperity, reach old age, and perhaps by reason of misfortune or otherwise come to a condition of want, the nation as a whole owes them something, not merely as a matter of charity but as a matter of right. If there is one factor that makes for the worries which beset us all it is the fear of the future. I believe Sir, that is a very real thing. The thought, I believe, that exists in the mind of every human being, even though that person may be in a position of affluence and prosperity, is that possibly he may not be able , to provide for himself when he reaches old age. If a provision such as this can help to relieve that situation, can help to dispel that thought in the minds of people, it will do a great deal more good than is accomplished merely by the monetary payments that are made; it will relieve during the whole course of a lifetime some of the fear to which I have just, referred.
Now, Sir, if the principle is right that the nation owes something to those who are no longer able to help themselves in their old

age, it becomes then merely a question as to how this relief shall be given. We have at the present time in most of our large municipalities, in the towns and cities, institutions known as poorhouses, houses of refuge or homes for old people, to take care of aged and indigent persons. We have such an institution in the city from which I come; in fact, I think it was one of the first established in the province. That institution has been improved from time to time until I believe it is to-day one of the best and most efficient of the kind. But in spite of such provision as this there still exists in the mind of almost everybody, and especially in the minds of those who feel that they may have to go there, a horror and a dread of being obliged to take refuge in an institution of that kind. That apprehension we should relieve, it seems to me, if it is possible to do so. We should allow the aged people to remain in their own homes where they may live self-respecting lives until such time as they come to the end of the road.
We have then the question whether the relief should come from provincial or from federal authorities. We have had some discussion this afternoon on that point. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) seemed to believe the matter is entirely one for the provinces. In view of the fact that there is some disagreement it seems to me it is not an unreasonable compromise to place the burden equally upon both the federal and the provincial governments. It is quite natural that the provinces should not be particularly anxious to assume this burden if they feel that the Dominion government is going to assume all the cost. In any case there is the proviso that the provinces are not obliged to enter into the scheme if they do not see fit to do so.
Other objections have been raised to the proposal as made. Some of them have considerable force. It seems to me it is our duty to consider these objections and to weigh them and see whether or not the preponderance is in favour of the scheme or otherwise. The three chief objections have been these: first, that the old age pension scheme makes for improvidence on the part of the public; secondly, the matter of expense, and thirdly, that to those provinces which do not choose to avail themselves of this legislation there comes the burden of supporting people who do not live in the provincial jurisdiction. In so far as the first is concerned-that this legislation will foster improvidence-I would say that I do not believe the character of the Canadian people is such that they will deliberately for a lifetime so
conduct themselves, be so wasteful and so fail to apply themselves to their work and to save something against old age, as to induce them, for the sake of some $20 a month, to become parasites upon the rest of the community after they reach the age of seventy years. With regard to the expense, I will admit that up until the present time I had felt that after the burdens imposed upon us on account of the war perhaps the time was not opportune to go into expense on this account. I believe from what I have heard that the expense will be quite moderate for some years, and after all I have come to the conclusion that this is a most worthy thing. It is right that something should be done, and that answers the objection almost entirely.
I will refer to another matter which has been mentioned this afternoon; that perhaps this government or any other succeeding government might very well economize along some other lines which I will not mention now-along lines much less important than old age pensions. With regard to the argument advanced more particularly by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White) I think he had particular reference to the province of Quebec when he said that those provinces which do not avail themselves of this legislation will be obliged to bear part of the burden for the other provinces. There is some force in that, but I would like to say, so far as the province of Quebec is concerned as I see it is represented in this House-and I do not say this for the purpose of flattery -that despite the fact that members from the province of Quebec were solidly Liberal in the last parliament and almost in the same position in this parliament, they have given us splendid examples of liberality and generosity. So far as the other provinces are concerned, they have never taken advantage of their own power to press their claims unduly, but have always sunk sectional advantage for the general good and I say that in justice to them. Even if there is some force in the argument of the hon. member for Mount Royal, is it not true that we never have any form of taxation which is equitably applied throughout the whole of Canada. It is practically impossible to apply taxation with entire equity; it is merely a matter of give and take in the interests of the whole Dominion. We might take some examples. We have in this House men elected from the Maritime provinces who attempt to place before parliament and to secure for their provinces some special consideration to which they think they are
