entitled. I might mention ' the matter of freight rates. We had during the recent campaign the argument of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) that special freight rates ought to be given to the west and also to eastern Canada. I am not going to argue as to the propriety, the advisability or the wisdom of that, but we have that suggestion. If lower rates were given to the extreme parts of Canada we would be in a position where one part of Canada would benefit at the expense of the other part.

I think that is hardly a fair statement of the position of the right hon. leader of the opposition. His position, as I understand it, on the question of freight rates for the Maritime provinces is not that the matter should be taken out of the jurisdiction of the railway commission, but that on certain well-defined principles there should be a public grant to give relief in some cases.

I was not making reference to the desire expressed by one member from Nova Scotia that the Intercolonial should be removed from the jurisdiction of the railway commission. I was referring entirely to the demand if I may call it a demand, that lower freight rates should be granted to the Maritime provinces as well as to the western provinces. If those demands were granted it would follow that the deficits of the national railways would be increased, and the burden of that would fall upon other portions of the Dominion. I am saying this not in criticism of the particular proposal at this time, but to show that it is utterly impossible to have taxation equitably applied throughout the whole of Canada, and that applies to the pensions now under discussion.
I have sometimes heard legislation of this kind described as socialistic. I am not a socialist, but I would say that so long as we operate under our present economic system, and perhaps it is best, in which every man fights for himself-and I was almost going to say, the devil take the hindmost-just so long as opportunities are unequal and the relative abilities of men are unequal-and they will always be- and so long as misfortune follows one man and not another, just so long will some of our people fall to the rear, and when they reach old age they will find that they must rely on assistance from their fellowmen in spite of their best efforts.
Legislation of this sort is sometimes regarded as sentimentalism, but it seems to me that in an age when the claim is made that we are now coming more and more to recognize the principles of what we may call the

brotherhood of man, and if there is -any sincerity in our professions of humanity, to say nothing about Christianity, it seems to me that a pension scheme such as this is a proof that the needs of the aged men and women are acknowledged to be a proper charge not only upon the conscience but also upon the material resources of the country.

It has been said this is a matter
that belongs or should belong exclusively to the provinces. Judged from the practice of the past I suppose that is true; and perhaps it is also true if we judge it from a strictly constitutional point of view. But whether or not that principle be applicable, I do not agree with those who say that this is a matter which belongs exclusively to the provinces and in which the Dominion of Canada has no part. There is not an hon. member in this House who does not know of a number of cases in his own part of the country where a man and a woman, perhaps in educating their children and bringing up their families to be good citizens, have made great sacrifices in the interests of Canada as a whole, and who, through no fault of their own, on account of unavoidable misfortune, find themselves at seventy years of age unable to maintain themselves. I do not agree with those who say that the Dominion of Canada as a whole owes nothing to these people; it seems to me that they have a very definite claim upon the federal treasury. I am in entire sympathy with the principle of old age pensions, although I think we will require to consider it very carefully and to make'alterations in the proposal as at present brought down.
The idea of old age pensions is not new in this country; we have had pensions fo, a great many years. We had them long before I had a seat in this House. We have had pensions for judges, pensions for soldiers-not merely those who served overseas but those also who served down in the Woods building or in other parts of Canada-yes, we have had these pensions for quite a while. I do not agree with the hon. gentleman who says that pensions discourage thrift. My observation is that the prospect of a pension has encouraged very materially the thrift of certain people in this country. They have looked forward anxiously and eagerly to the day when they will draw that pension.

They paid for it,
but the hon. member seems to ignore that fact.

If my hon. friend will wait a while, I will not ignore

Old Age Pensions
that fact, or the fact that he is a pensioner. Let us take, for instance, the matter of pensions to judges. This is not the first time that I have raised my voice in objection to these pensions. It did not do any good on former occasions, and I do not suppose it will do any good now. There are in this House too many lawyers for that; they are looking after themselves sufficiently and they are, I presume, looking forward to the time when they will also pull down pensions as judges. I would not be at all surprised if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was looking forward to pulling down a pension.
I notice from the Auditor General's report we are paying $15,333.12 in pensions to three judges of the Supreme Court of Canada. Hon. members will note that they do not let u,p on the cents; they pull down even the 12 cents. There are twelve Ontario judges drawing $41,666.80 a year, and fourteen Quebec judges drawing $77,003.26 a year. Among them one judge who draws down a pension of $8,000 a year. Three get $7,999.92 each; two get $6,999.96 each; three get $6,000 each; two get $7,000 each and two others get $4,666.66 each. So it goes on. In Nova Scotia four judges draw $13,600; in New Brunswick four judges draw $13,166; in Manitoba four draw $13,663; in British Columbia two draw $3,833, and in the Yukon one draws $4,999. In this way there is an amount of $184,397.71 being paid out in pensions to these poor, unfortunate, indigent judges of this country. Of course the Supreme court judges and other judges in Cana la work at such a small salary that they could never lay by anything for their old age, so they are provided for in this way.
When I refer to these pensioned judges I recall an hon. gentleman who graced the floor of this parliament for some years, who was a cabinet minister, who drew his sessional indemnity as a member of parliament, his remuneration as a cabinet minister and at the same time his pension of $4,666.66 a year. The reason why this judge was retired from the bench was because the work was too strenuous for him. He wanted a life of ease, and so he came into parliament. In order to be sure that the work would be extremely easy for him he took a cabinet position where he would have nothing at all to do. I recall another hon. gentleman who had a seat in this House for a number of years and who sat on the other side. I want to refer to the two so as to balance things up properly. This gentleman held the position of leader of the opposition; he almost became Prime Minister of the Dominion of Canada, but not quite. He was voted down on a memorable
occasion when the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Mackenzie King) received the highest vote and was selected. This hon. gentleman had retired from the bench; the work got too strenuous for him; he could not stand the strain and he retired under a pension. He came into this House and he drew his sessional indemnity, his salary as leader of the opposition and his pension as a retired judge. He carried on here for a while, but this life got tame for him and he went back again to the strenuous life on the bench. I do not know whether or not he is now drawing his first pension, but I am sure that the fact of a pension being ahead of him will not discourage his thrift by any means. He will look forward to that eagerly. Some say: If you want a pension scheme, it will involve a large amount of money. They capitalize that amount of money and it amounts to so many million dollars capitalized. If you capitalize at four per cent the pensions now being paid to judges who worked for a bare living when they were on the bench and never could lay anything by for their old age, it will amount to pretty nearly $5,000,000.
We have in this country another class of people who are drawing down pensions, and this is the cl as? that the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) wanted me to go into details about. We have a number of military men, some of whom risked their lives overseas and some of whom risked their health in offices in Ottawa. Of course those who came back from overseas, who lived through that strenuous life, are drawing a pension, and rightly so. But those who lived through the stress and strain of office work at Ottawa, and were almost martyrs to the war by the great work that they were doing here and the long hours they were putting in, made application for and obtained pensions. I think the hon. member for Rimouski is one who is in that glorified class.

hon. member wishes to be fair. Does he remember the services rendered by the hon. member for Rimouski in the South African war?

Yes, I
remember that very well. I would not detract a particle from any of the military glory of the hon. member for Rimouski or the Solicitor General either, for that matter.
I am not in this at all.

I would not specially refer to this if the hon. member for Rimouski had not interrupted me a while ago

and called for it, but I do not suppose the pension of that hon. gentleman had anything to do with the South African war.

That is where the hon.
gentleman is wrong.

I am not
finding fault with these military gentlemen for drawing pensions, any more than I am finding fault with judges for doing so. The fault does not lie with them; they could not get the pensions if there was not
9 p.m. a law on the statute books giving them pensions. But when we are considering whether or not we shall hand out $240 a year-not even a bare living-to a man who has lived in and served this country just as well as the judges and military men have, in view of these figures with regard to the pensions that these men are drawing, I say that so long as we have on the statute books of this country laws that enable judges to be retired at six, seven and eight thousand dollars a year and military men to retire, while they are in splendid health and good physical condition, on pensions of several thousand dollars a year, I will support on every occasion a pension to give something to old men of seventy years of age. I do not want to use any harsh terms in regard to these pensioners, but I believe I would be justified in referring, not by any means to all these pensions, not by any means to a majority of them, but to some of them, as nothing more nor less than glorified graft. That is the way it appears to me at all events. 1 think we should consider this whole matter carefully, going over the acts that provide pensions to men who, in my judgment, are not entitled to them, and wipe those acts off the statute book. Let us get down to sanity in this matter and if necessary give these men a decent, reasonable salary; but let us remove these provisions from the law.
I would be the last to raise any objection to giving them an edequate salary. These gentlemen seem anxious enough to take judgeships when they are offered, and in my opinion we should give them a remuneration sufficient to enable them to provide for their old age. But if out of their salaries they cannot make that provision for themselves, then I do not think that they should be given pensions. It is ridiculous that certain men who have occupied positions in which they have received large salaries should be given pensions that enable them to live in luxury while others who have served the country equally well, even though in humbler capacity, receive nothing at all and are obliged occasionally to go to the poorhouse.

The present proposal is to grant a pension of $240 to men seventy years of age and up. Out of that the pensioner must provide a roof over his head besides clothing, food and fuel, and it is not unreasonable to suppose that he will be ill occasionally and incur expenses for doctor's services and so forth. All that he must provide out of $240 a year. Well, we may get a good deal of patting on the back from people for giving the indigent a pension of $240, but I do not think there is a member in this House who does not realize that this sum is altogether inadequate. I am in a position to obtain information from my own constituency to prove what I say. Last Saturday I had a conversation with the county clerk of the county of Frontenac in regard to this very matter, and I got from him certain information bearing on the cost of running the House of Providence and the House of Refuge, both in the city of Kingston. These two institutions provide food and shelter for the indigent of the county. I have in my hand the figures given me by the county clerk in regard to ten men and five women inmates. I find that the cost for clothes, tobacco and little necessaries for the men ranged from as low as $12.40 to as high as $24.39 over a period of three months. The county pays a straight fee of $4.80 per person per week, and taking into consideration maintenance, cost of clothing and so on, the average for the ten men was $26.65 per month. That, I think, is the lowest possible cost of maintaining these people. That would be a matter of $320 a year, or $80 more than the pension which it is proposed to give under this scheme.	.
I presume that the figures I have given for the county of Frontenac would be about the same as the cost in other parts of Ontario and probably very much the same as in every other section of the Dominion. Now, bearing in mind that the poor who are kept in these institutions are given, besides the shelter that is afforded them, the necessary medical attendance and all that, I am convinced that, in view of the fact that the lowest possible cost of maintaining the individual in such a place amounts to $320 per annum, anyone who receives only $240, out of which he must provide his own shelter, fuel, food, clothing and everything else, will find it exceedingly difficult to keep himself on that sum. The $240 will not nearly keep body and soul together.
There is a good deal to be said in favour of the institutions. When these people are taken ill, if they are living in the country some distance away, who is going to look after them? [DOT] If, however, they are in an institution they are cared for at a time when it is

Old Age Pensions
imperative that they be looked after. There is this danger about giving these pensions, that where the pensioner is living by himself and maintaining or trying to maintain himself on $240 a year, people who otherwise would take an iterest in him will say: "Well, we are under no obligation. He is receiving a government pension, and he is supposed to be able to live on that." Now, we have a duty to these old people. There is no question about that, and we should not shirk the responsibility. I am entirely in agreement with the proposal that this obligation should be shared by the provinces, but I fancy the government will be well advised to be in no great hurry with this bill. I am not sure that it would not pay to wait perhaps another year, if by so doing we could obtain a definite expression of opinion and perhaps get all the provinces to come under the scheme. Others may differ from me in that regard. Certainly it is perfectly logical that the province that does not come in will be obliged to contribute towards expenses from which it will receive no money. True, as has been already stated, we should multiply instances in other matters where this discrepancy has occurred throughout the country.
A word in conclusion. I am in sympathy with old age pensions, and I believe that a duty does rest on the Dominion in that regard. I believe, further, that this duty has been accentuated, so far as we are concerned, by the recent war. Perhaps I might cite a case by -way of illustration. Two or three weeks ago an old man, though a man not so very old in point of years-he is about sixty-seven or sixty-eight-wrote asking me to appeal to the pension board to see whether I could not get him a pension. The reason he advanced was that his only son went over to the war, and he was alone in the world, his wife being dead. When the son went to the war this man, who was a carpenter and in good health, was looking after himself and was perfectly confident of his ability to do so. Had the son said to his father, "Now, father, I will send you some of my pay," I have no doubt the father would have said, "No, I do not want your pay; I can make my own money"-and so he could, at that time. But he is not in a position to make any money to-day. His only son lies buried in France. I appealed on his behalf- I arn not blaming the Board of Pension Commissioners; they have their regulations-and was told that if this man's son had sent any of his pay to his father they would have taken that as evidence that the father depended upon the son for support, but inasmuch
as the son did not send any of his pay, the father has no claim upon the government of Canada for any assistance. That is the situation; I can get nothing for him, and he is not in a position to get anything for himself. That man lives in the province of Ontario. Am 1 to be told that the obligation rests entirely on Ontario to provide for that man in his old age? Was it only for Ontario that his son was fighting? No, Mr. Speaker; his son went overseas and fought for the Dominion of Canada. If that son had been spared he would be taking care of his father to-day. I have no doubt in my mind, Mr. Speaker, that the Dominion of Canada is under obligation to that man, to a certain extent at least. He is very close to seventy years of age, and the government should provide some assistance for his declining years. There are many cases like this, I have no doubt, all over the country; the situation has been aggravated by the war. That being the case, there is a duty, an obligation, a responsibility resting upon this Dominion seriously to consider this matter and to see what we can do in the way of making the declining years of the old people reasonably comfortable.

Mr. Speaker, at this late hour I do not wish to detain the House very long on this subject, but now that the principle olf old age pensions has been generally accepted there seems to be no reason why this legislation should not be unanimously accepted by the House. Other parts of the empire, Great Britain and Australia, have accepted the principle of old age pensions, and Canada is in duty bound to follow the example so shown. Old age pensions are to-day accepted by almost all civilized nations; the only objection we have heard against the scheme, so far, has been the refusal of some of the provinces to co-operate with the government in putting such a measure into execution. So far as my own constituency is concerned-a constituency composed very largely of wage earners and old pioneers -the sentiment generally is in favour of this legislation.
If amongst our population there is one class deserving of consideration, it is that class of old pioneers who spent the best parts of their lives in developing the fringes of our civilization. We have such cases in my constituency. Wo have old settlers who, after labouring for many years, have had years of bad crops, have met with misfortune and have had their farms taken from them by foreclosure, or have been forced to sell at prices which did not assure them of a livelihood for their remaining years.

We have also a class of people in the north country who have contributed a great deal to the development of the country, and those are the people engaged in the lumbering industry. The lumberman of the north has often been accused of not being thrifty, but even in our days of prosperity, when 'he standard of living was improving throughout the country and the scale of wages of all organized labour was rising, the man employed in the lumber industry had to be satisfied with the very lowest wage. In our House of Refuge in the city of North Bay one of the best managed and most progressive houses of refuge in-the north country, we find that of its inmates a large majority spent a good many years in the lumber camps. These conditions exist, and it is the duty of the Dominion as well as that of the provinces to see that those citizens of Canada are not left to shift for themselves, but are given a certain measure of assistance.
That also applies to a very large class of unskilled labour. It is said to-day that the standard of living amongst wage earners is steadily increasing. While that is true; while the standard of living is increasing among those engaged in certain occupations, or members of labour organizations, the unskilled labourer has found it very much harder to keep up with that rising standard of living. It is among that class that you will find the man of seventy who is unable to provide for his last years. Our industrial system of to-day is called a capitalistic system, and it will be said to have failed if the great army of wage earners who have contributed their share towards the development and progress of our country are not fully taken care of, as well as those in the higher spheres of life. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I am going to support this resolution.

I desire to offer a few observations only, Mr. Speaker, with reference to this matter. First of all, I think there has been some misapprehension on the part of some speakers as to what the real situation is. In the first place, it is quite clear, although it has never been exactly determined, that the provinces have perhaps sole jurisdiction with respect to the granting of old age pensions, and secondly, that this parliament has power by the grant of money to supplement the action of the provinces in that regard. The various committees of this House that have dealt with this matter apparently were entirely moved by those considerations, and in 1925, on the 16th day of June last year, the committee that had made the recommendations for pen-

sions legislation saw fit to make another recommendation to this House, and that recommendation is one which I submit the government should give effect to. It is the recommendation of the committee of which the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) was a member. It is a recommendation which in my judgment recognizes the real difficulty of this situation. It is a recommendation which, if departed from, .will bring about the condition of affairs to which the hon. gentleman from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) referred this afternoon.
May I refer to the Journals for the 16th of June, 1925? I observe that-
Mr. Raymond, from pthe special committee, appointed on the 1st of May last to make an inquiry into an old age pension system for Canada, to which was referred the correspondence arising from the proposals recommended to parliament on the 1st of July, 1924, for co-operative action on the part of the federal government and the governments of the several provinces, ha* the honour to report as follows.
After reviewing the correspondence and the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice the report proceeds:
The enactment of such legislation would, however, involve the assumption by the Dominion of obligations involving heavy expenditures with regard to a matter which does not fall specifically within the Dominion field of legislation.
Having given very careful consideration to the opinion submitted by the Department of Justice, and also to the respective views of the different provinces, your committee have come to the following conclusions:
Firstly, that if the Dominion government were to proceed now with a scheme of old age pensions, it would have to be prepared to bear the entire expense, which would approximately amount to twenty-three million (123,000,000) dollars annually, according to the data obtained in your committee's investigations.
Secondly, that in view of the present financial conditions and heavy taxation of Canada, your committee would not feel warranted at the present moment in recommending such a large additional expenditure, annually.
Thirdly, that this measure of social reform, in the opinion of your committee, is very important, and
Fourthly, that since it is the opinion of the Department of Justice that the matter is one coming under the jurisdiction of the provinces, although open to assistance from the federal government, your committee, therefore, strongly recommend :-
1.	That the federal government arrange with the premiers of the different provinces for a conference to be held during the coming recess of parliament at which an old age pension system shall be given the fullest consideration with a view to securing co-operative action, and that the report of the said conference be laid on the table at the next session of parliament for future consideration and action.
2.	That the chairman of your committee, and one other of its members who would be familiar with the subject matter, be invited to attend the said conference.
3.	That a copy of this report be forwarded to each premier o-f the several provinces.
Now may I direct the attention of this House to the fact that that report, accepted and adopted by parliament in June last, is

a report of the committee of which the hon. member for Comox-Albemi was a member, and that report clearly indicates, as clearly as words can, that this parliament should not proceed with this measure unless and until the provinces had agreed upon a co-operative system with respect to pensions throughout Canada. It is quite clear that as the election came shortly after, there was no likelihood of a conference being called between that time and the end of the year. There has been no opportunity for calling a conference since, and I do submit therefore that on the records of this parliament, upon the report of the committee, of which two hon. gentlemen at least of this House were then members, it is clearly apparent that it was not intended, contemplated, nor even thought by the committee that we should have an old age pension scheme put in force in Canada unless, as the committee points out, the Dominion government were prepared to bear the whole responsibility and pay the $23,000,000 annually in its entirety. The reasons for it were so admirably dealt with this afternoon by other speakers that I shall not refer to them, but as the hon. member for Labelle pointed out, if all the provinces did not agree, if one of the provinces did and another did not, and the citizens of the province that did not agree went into the province that did agree, then the new provincial home would be called upon to become responsible for the payment of part of the pension of those newcomers.
Now it is clear that parliament in 1925, and the committee that gave to this matter such unremitting care, as mentioned by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi, were clearly, and the members severally were of the opinion that there should be no old age pension legislation by this parliament unless the various provinces had agreed and had arrived at a conclusion with respect to it, and as the correspondence indicated that they were not agreed, and as the minister stated this afternoon there has been no further correspondence, therefore it follows that this parliament should not proceed with this matter at this time, and, Mr. Speaker, I do venture to plead with my friends opposite not to urge the government to proceed with it at this time. Faulty legislation placed upon the statute books the effect of which is to bring . about chaos is very much to be deprecated. Anyone who has followed the course of legislation in any country, especially legislation of this character, will realize that where you rely solely and entirely upon experiments you have nothing but political action following political action, and what was intended to be a great benefit has in many instances been a positive disadvantage to the very class it was intended to benefit.
Let me for a moment point out that since this committee made its investigation, two changes of the utmost importance have taken place in the world. I refer first of all to the ' change that has taken place in England, and I venture to ask my friends who are interested in this matter to turn to volume 184 of the English Hansard, page 74, and read the speech of the Right Hon. Neville Chamberlain in moving the adoption of the new system in England, the system that now obtains and prevails there. That speech was opened on the 18th of May, 1925, and many months passed by before the legislation in question was finally adopted. I commend the speech to gentlemen who desire to observe the reasons that brought about the change in England, and which resulted in the old non-contributory system being superseded by a contributory system.
Is the hon. gentleman correct in his facts, that the other system has been superseded?

The word superseded I think is the correct word, because Mr. Chamberlain has pointed out that the old system which provided for pensions at the age of seventy, and which was a non-contributory system, was to be merged under certain conditions in the new scheme, which provides for pensions at sixty-five, and which is contributory in its character.

I happen to have a copy of the act in my hand, and I do not think the hon. gentleman's statement is entirely correct. What has happened there is that the old system remains as it was, but it has been added to by a contributory system, as the hon. gentleman has just stated.

I am sorry the hon. gentleman has not, in my judgment, correctly observed all the facts, because I shall read in a moment from the address made by Mr. Chamberlain at Birmingham and broadcast throughout the kingdom, explaining the operation of the new system and its effect upon the old. It only takes a single page, and I shall read it because it is of importance to this House to observe how in Great Britain they have seen the faults of the non-contributory system; and in Australia, in 1925, at the very time this House was considering the report of the special committee, a recommendation was made that their non-contributory system should be changed to con-

tributary system; and in Belgium, where they had a non-contributory system, the same recommendation has been made and put into effect. The reasons for it are admirably explained by the late Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain in a speech which he made at Birmingham in 1906, and which was quoted by [DOT] his son in moving the second reading of the old age pension bill in England last year. The late Mr. Joseph Chamberlain said:
All I have done in reference to this matter is to express my own sense of the necessity of enabling the industrious working people to make a betteT provision for old age-
Observe the words:
-to enable "working people" to make a better provision for old age, and to put before the working people of this country one or two circumstances, two plans in particular, which I have said and which I maintain are perfectly simple and clearly to be understood, which are within the reach of the working class of this country. . . That is my part in the matter, and I still think that this better provision ought to be, and should be made by the House of Commons. But it is not, and never will be so far as I am concerned, a proposal for anything in the nature of a universal old age pension, which, I believe, is impracticable from the point of view of its expense and which I believe, is immoral and undesirable from the point of view of its influence upon thrift and industry.
That in 1906 expressed the considered opinion of, the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, and his son, in moving the second reading of the most recent legislation of that character in England, gave expression to his father's sentiments by quoting the language I have just read, and upon that predicated a measure of reform that is now part of the legislation of England.
I do contend, Sir, that in this new country, with our great undeveloped natural resources, with our necessarily very large number of young people, it is of the utmost importance that we should have some contributory system of pensions rather than a non-contributory system. I say that for two reasons: First, because there is nothing more serious in a new country than that men should grow up with the idea or thought that they are to rely upon what is now called in England the dole; and secondly; that habits of thrift and economy should be encouraged and developed among the people if we are to take our place among the great nations of the world. I am convinced of that. The late Sir Richard Cartwright, who occupied so commanding a place in . parliament, gave to this matter, as you will remember, a very great deal of time and attention. When he found himself in a position where the government of which he was a member could command the support of parliament, he introduced and caused to be passed through parliament the system with 
respect to annuities that we have upon our statute books. He did it to encourage habits of thrift. He did it that the young might, by saving small sums in their younger days, be able to have a fair and decent annuity in their old age.
Now, I will take the trouble to quote a few figures, and I trust I shall not weary the House by doing so. Let me put this case to the House: Assume that a young man of twenty desires to provide for his old age. If he goes into the government annuity office in this city, which is maintained at the public expense but which is not used so much as it should be, and desires to purchase from the government of this country an annuity, and if he will for each month during the year 1926 pay the small sum of 84 cents-a little lesi, I think-he will when he becomes seventy years of age have an annuity of a dollar a month.

in the sense that Canada is federal?

I do not think any of
them are federal in the sense that the United States or Canada is federal, except Germany.
Now to proceed. In the United States of America the matter has engaged the attention of many of the states. I think the state of Arizona enacted the first old age pension law. I commend hon. members to a consideration of a report that has probably engaged the minds of more thoughful men for a longer period of time than any report yet made on this continent. I refer to the report on old age pensions by the commission on pensions appointed by the legislature of the state of Massachusetts and printed in November, 1925.

Old Age Pensions

That is the fullest exposition of the history of old age pensions that I think can easily be found, and in the appendix commencing at page 2S1 there is a full review of pensions in all the various countries. I was amazed to find that Germany, where they have a federal system of government-in point of fact it is fourth among the federal systems of the world-expended in the last year of which I have a report, over $103,000,000 in pensions, and that Great Britain expended only a million more, making $104,000,000. In Australia, with the non-contributory system, they find the pressure of politicians upon the government so strong that a royal commission investigating the matter has recommended a contributory system. Why? For reasons that I am sure must commend themselve to the government and to hon. members in this House. Every time a general election came round the constituent got busy for an increase of the monthly allowance. No contributions being made, it was an incentive to idleness, and in many respects did much to bring about conditions which the people of Australia very greatly deprecated; so much so that in the end they recommended that the contributory system be relied upon in order that the men who demand more money shall make larger contributions.
There are many other facts to which I should like to allude, and which I possibly may refer to if the measure goes to a second reading, but I rose to-night to plead with the administration and more with the members of this House who are forcing the legislation upon the administration-I do not use the words in any offensive sense-the desirability of not now passing this resolution. I implore them to give to this matter further time and consideration.. I ask |them not to hurry forward the legislation, and I promise them that so long as I am in the House-and I think I know the sentiments of some of my hon. friends on this side of the House-we will give every assistance we can in the way of suggestions or useful constructive criticism.
I want to see in this country a system providing for old age deferred annuities, for old age pension. But in this new young country, with its resources untouched and undeveloped, where we are endeavouring to develop a hardy spirit of enterprise on the part of our citizens, where we want them to look upon the government as an instrument for their well-being and not something on which they are to depend for sustenance, I do plead with the government to give the opportunity which the committee of last year promised would be given, namely, the calling together

of representatives of all the provinces in order that a conclusion may be arrived at that will be fitting for so great and important a subject. This House has not been called upon to deal with any matter more important nor any subject more far-reaching in its operations and in its effect. Mr. Churchill in his great speech dealt with this subject, and Mr. Chamberlain said, "You cannot speak of this matter from the standpoint of to-day; it is what is going to happen fifty years from now." Mr. Churchill pointed out that with the prolongation of human life by the application of scientific modern methods; with the improvement in the health of the citizens, we will have a longer life and there will be an increased financial obligation upon the state. And I ask my friends who are so bent upon putting this through to pause, to consider, to weigh, and to ask whether or not we are lighty to disregard the recommendations of the committee that gave such time, such consideration and such thought to this matter.
I know that the right hon. leader of the government has given much time, thought and consideration to this question. Anyone who has read his work, Industry and Humanity, must be impressed with the fact that this is a social problem in which he is deeply interested, and I do ask him whether or not he believes that legislation hastily considered and placed upon the statute books of the country, pledging the credit of the country, against the recommendation of the committee, placing upon posterity a burden that cannot be easily shaken off is in the best interests of Canada. The great difficulty in a matter of this kind is that once you enact a law and place it on the statute book, and once you incur financial responsibility, you cannot lightly shake it off, as you can your overcoat. These are the obligations that stick and remain with us, and I do ask in the name of all those who are desirous of bringing about the best form of legislation, who know that hurried legislation very often is worse than none at all, who realize, if they will take the time to read the report made in the state of Massachusetts, the debate in the English House and the discussions that there took place, the far-reaching consequences of these proposals I ask them all to pause and consider. I wonder if hon. members would like to hear the message broadcast by Mr. Chamberlain. It is not very long.
Go ahead.

and, in a very short time, an expenditure of $40,000,000 per annum, an expenditure entirely too large for us to entertain at the present time. I think the government, therefore, will be well advised perhaps to release the whip on its own members and let the opinion of the House as a whole determine whether or not it is desirable at this session to push into this matter or, in the light of a subsequent conference between the provincial and Dominion authorities, arrive at a conclusion which will enable us to place on our statute books legislation of a character that will redound to the credit of this country and that will maintain the confidence and self-respect of the future citizens of this Dominion by encouraging the practice of economy and thrift, while providing for the aged of to-day by suitable contributions to provincial schemes.
Do I understand that the Massachusetts report recommended the contributory system?

No. The Massachusetts
report, by a division of three to two, recommended a non-contributory system for reasons they gave, but they stated that it must be at once met by increased taxation such as a $2 poll tax upon its citizens and an increase of one-half of one per cent of the income tax to raise an annual sum of $6,500,000.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there is an understanding, although it has not been formally expressed, that the House will not sit quite as late to-night as it did last night, but that we will adjourn shortly after ten o'clock. For that reason I shall not attempt to speak at any length on the resolution which is before the House, but I should like to follow my hon. friend in a few words in reference to some of the points he has brought to the attention of hon. members in, I must say, an admirable manner.
_ Speaking generally on the question of social insurance, of which old age pensions is one form, I agree entirely with the point of view which my hon. friend has expressed, that a contributory system is the proper one to adopt. I think it is desirable to enlist not merely the sympathies but the active participation of individuals in schemes of social insurance that are intended for their benefit. But while I entertain that view, I think a study of the question will go to show that, with respect to old age pensions, particularly their immediate application in countries that have systems of social insurance to-day, the schemes have been intitiated not 
under a contributory system but by a method such as is being proposed at the present time. It is important that the principle on the part of the state that there is an obligation be acknowledged at the outset. I will not assert the theory that the state owes a man a living or any part of a living, but rather that social justice demands, under the system in which industry is carried on to-da.y, where the rights of private property are recognized to the full, that there should be means whereby individuals who are not possessed of and have little means of acquiring private property to any extent should not be obliged to suffer unaided the handicaps of such a system, but that the state itself should recognize some obligations towards them as a consequence of the manner in which industry is carried on. If we were legislating as my hon. friend has suggested, for young people of the age of ten or twelve; if we were providing an old age scheme for page boys about the House, for schoolboys and girls, then it would be wise to lay emphasis upon the importance of a contribution on their part towards a system intended to help to maintain them in their old age. But I take it that this House at the present time, in discussing old age pensions, is not thinking of young people of ten, twenty or thirty years of age or even of persons of forty or fifty years of age. We are thinking more particularly of that large body of men and women now in Canada who are approaching the age of seventy years. We have in mind those between the ages of sixty and seventy who are finding it difficult to get the assurance that their declining years are not going to be spent in dependence on charity. It is for such people that we are legislating at the moment. We have in view men and women in Canada between the ages of fifty and seventy who are facing actual concrete conditions as they prevail in this Dominion today. That embraces hundreds, yes thousands of men and women who are earning their livelihood in factories and workshops, in different forms of clerical employment, as well as the thousands who as pioneers have contributed so largely to the upbuilding of the Dominion but who in their effort to bring up their families have been unable to lay aside any sum of money sufficient to maintain them in their old age.

Does the right hon. gentleman realize, when he says that he is dealing with people between the ages of fifty and seventy, that this involves the maintenance of this principle for twenty years, and that at the expiration of that time the

Old Age Pensions
actuarial figures would place the country's responsibility at a sum upwards of $40,000,000?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will make
clear what I have in mind. My hon. friend has discussed in a way that is helpful the legislation that has been passed in Great Britain as recently as within the last year. But he might have emphasized at the same time the fact that England introduced her old age pension scheme in 1909. It was amended in 1911 and again in 1919, having been maintained all this while as a non-contributory scheme. But what has developed in Great Britain in the recent past? Alongside old age pensions there has grown up a system of social insurance applying to many phases of life-insurance against unemployment, insurance against invalidism, insurance against accident, insurance against disease and insurance in the way of maternity benefits, and so forth-a great mass of social insurance all of which relates to the hazards of industry incident to that large part of the population engaged in industrial pursuits of one kind or another. And recent legislation has assembled these various forms of social insurance into one great compendium, so to speak, and linked up the old age pensions sj'stem therewith.
In this country, I should like to see the annuities plan which, as my hon. friend has said, was inaugurated by Sir Richard Cartwright, developed into a comprehensive system of social insurance. But I do not believe that [DOT]this can be accomplished solely by the federal government ; it would have to receive the cooperation of the provinces. We must in some way establish that link between the provinces and the Dominion which will conduce to the working out of a great social insurance scheme along these lines. That will not be achieved in a year; as in other countries it will require time. The old age pension phase of the question is one that has an immediate bearing in respect of people of advanced years. Surely, then, we shall not be running any great risk so far as future generations are concerned if we put upon the statutes this year legislation which will hold out an inducement to the provinces to come together in conference for the purpose of discussing social legislation generally.
In the course of the debate to-day reference has been made to the old age pensions scheme as though it were something related particularly to inmates of poorhouses. I am inclined to feel that there is no class in human society to-day that has not in its numbers a very considerable percentage of persons who are living in constant dread of the moment when, in their advanced years,
they will be thrown upon their children or upon society for support. I fancy there are many members of the legal and medical professions, clergymen and their wives, besides numbers of civil servants, clerks in all branches of occupation, who as they approach the age of fifty or six-ty find that in a very few years' time every dollar which they have been able to put by gradually disappears, while simultaneously their earning capacity has been very seriously impaired. We are living under industrial conditions very different from those which the world has known heretofore. We are living in an age of keen competition, not only as between locality and locality, between state and state, between province and province, or between countries, but between continent and continent, and conditions affecting one quarter of the world are bound to react very soon in another quarter. Men and women, therefore, through no fault of their own find themselves thrown out of their occupations and unable to gain a livelihood. Consider industry for a moment. The processes of industrial life to-day hinge more and more upon a division of labour, and in an ever-increasing degree individuals are becoming specialists. The whole development of power, from water-power to steam and from steam to electricity, has been in the nature of an intensifying process which makes it impossible for men and women, once they have attained a certain age, to hold their own in the competitive arena. Consequently -they are thrown to one side by a younger generation better adapted to the tasks which they have been performing and left to seek work in other directions. We all know this, and, knowing it, I think we feel the necessity of making some *provision whereby men and women after they have done the best they can through life, should be freed, on attaining the age of seventy, from that fear of dependence upon charity which carries with it a sort of stigma at the end of a life of honourable activity.
My hon. friend said that the report which the committee brought in offered a reason to Which the government at the moment should give heed. He left, I think, the impression that the report suggested that this work was only to be gone on with when all the provinces should agree to co-operate. I do not read the report in that way. I venture to say that had the committee reported that we should wait until all the provinces agreed to co-operate in any scheme of insurance the committee would virtually have declared that in its opinion the question should not be considered for some years to come. Here is
Old Age Pensions

the clause of the report which my hon. friend read, but let me direct his attention to the wording of it:
That the federal government arrange with the premiers of the different provinces for a conference to be held during the coming recess of parliament at which an old age pension system shall be given the fullest consideration with a view to securing co-operative action, and that the report of the said conference be laid on the table at the next session of parliament for future consideration and action.
"Future consideration and action".

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but the report says, "at which an old age pension system shall be given the fullest consideration, with a view to securing co-operative action-". I venture to say that it will be necessary, before this scheme is worked out in an effective manner, to have a conference of the premiers or other representatives of the different provinces, to consider how the provinces can most effectively work in under the plan that is here proposed, but the thing that will help bring about co-operative action is having something concrete to lay before them.

The report has it the
other way. "That the report of the said conference be laid on the table at the next session of parliament for future consideration and action".

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am quite prepared to admit that that had reference to a conference. If a conference had been called last summer that action would have been taken, but as my hon. friend knows it was impossible to have a conference last summer, which makes the laying of a report on the table impossible at the present time. It does not, however, make impossible the preparation by this government of a carefully drafted method of assisting the provinces in an old age pension scheme, and then, when that plan is adopted, an invitation to the provinces to meet with members of the federal government to consider regulations for the carrying out of the plan. That procedure does not in any way preclude the conference; indeed, it will help bring about the conference in an effective way. It practically suggests that a step of that kind will be taken and ought to be taken.
In regard to legislation of this kind which necessarily is in part a matter of provincial legislation, I agree with my hon. friend that so far as the federal government is concerned our du'ty is largely that of assisting such of the provinces as are willing to undertake such a

scheme as is proposed. If. that is true, I think it follows that it is very desirable to have, sc far as it is possible to have it, uniformity among the different provinces in any scheme adopted. An unfortunate feature which arises from the division between the provinces on matters relating to industry is that there are so many different standards in the different provinces. One of "the greatest needs in the industrial life of Canada to-day is that the standards governing industrial relations should be more or less identical as between one province and another. That can only be brought about by some kind of action on the part of the federal government leading to co-operation between the federal government and the provinces and among the different provinces themselves. I submit that this scheme of old age pensions as here drafted will have that effect. It will be the natural thing to ask the representatives of the provincial governments to meet with the department of the federal government which may be administering the old age pensions plan, to discuss further its details, and to consider the regulations for its effective operation.
I did not really mean to take any part in the discussion this evening, but I felt that I would like to follow my hon. friend in one or two points which he developed. I hope I have shown him that they are factors which the government did not fail to take into account and did not overlook, but that so far as the purpose of the immediate legislation is concerned, it looks to providing a pension for men and women of the generation that is passing away, or will have passed away in the course of a very few years. That is primarily what we are considering at this moment, and in considering men and women of that category we will, I think, be taking the first necessary step to bring about that larger measure of contributory social insurance which is one of the great needs of our time.	/
Would the right hon. gentleman permit a question, or rather two questions in one?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.

Does it not follow that
before this legislation can be made applicable the provinces will have to pass legislation? Secondly, will not such legislation to be passed by the provinces have to conform, generally speaking, to the provisions of this federal act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.

Old Age Pension$

Therefore would it not
be better to have the conference prior to the passing of this legislation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think my
hon. friend, if he looks into his heart of hearts, will agree with me when I say that if we are in a position to put before representatives of the provinces a plan which has been drafted and carefully considered, and an act passed by this parliament, and to invite the attention of the provinces to what may be essential in the way of amendment to it or its relation to their own legislation, a measure of cooperation can be obtained that would not be possible if the provinces were simply brought together without any concrete legislation before them for consideration. I think what will happen is this: under this legislation, which I hope will be passed this session, until the provinces themselves undertake to conform to the regulations here laid down, not a dollar will be taken out of the public treasury. That will mean that the provinces will have to consider whether or not this is an act they will care to come under.
All the provinces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, any province which cares to adopt legislation of that character. In that regard may I say that as between the different provinces I fail to see where there is a distinction to be drawn between the money voted by this parliament say for the purposes of immigration, which may go to place a man or woman in any one of the provinces, and money voted for preserving the individual, no matter in what part of the Dominion he may be found. Human beings are the greatest of the resources of the country. What we are here considering is human life. An individual, no matter which province he is in, is an asset to the Dominion as a whole, and it is from that point of view that the Dominion is, I think, considering this matter.
May I point out that in the case of an immigrant he becomes a producer, while old age pensions are given to indigents?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend has presented a point of view which I hope this House will consider. He says that one man is a producer and the other an indigent. I have here a letter which I would like to read to the House. It was written by an elderly lady in Alberta in June, 1925. I will not read the whole letter, because it has some references to matters which I think need not be
placed on record at the moment, although I shall be glad to show the entire letter to my hon. friend if he so desires. The letter begins by drawing my attention to the fact that this parliament recently voted a large sum of money by way of an annuity to one who had been a distinguished member of parliament. It points out that sums of money were voted by this parliament to cover some of the expenses incident to the visit of a great general from overseas and for other purposes, and it continues:
I am impelled to write you on the old age pension. The poor old people, the pioneers of Canada, who have worked hard against great odds and nothing like a salary in return, have to stand aside while these large sums are disbursed. It will be extremely inconsistent should the old age pension bill not pass very soon, with the powers that be in parliament.
The letter next refers to a sum of money that had been raised for assistance im some connection, and then goes on:
Worthy these gentlemen may all be, but it gives one the notion that if men getting such immense salaries and sums of money cannot make provision for a time when they cannot work, how possibly can a working man do so? It would be a boon if something can be done to relieve the hardships of the working class, especially when they reach an age which makes it difficult to live. Most of whom cannot work at an advanced age, and are not wanted at work either. My husband is turned 72, and is as yet strong and able to work, and does work hard. Still he is feeling the effects of age, along with work, which he has never shirked, but has had his share of trouble and losses, making him feel that he, along with others, deserve some consideration from the country.
I say to my hon. friend from Mount Royal (Mr. White) that the woman who wrote that letter was not an indigent; her husband, even had he been unable to d*o any work, is not to be classel as an indigent; they are two people who have helped to make this country what it is; they have helped to make the wealth of this country.
The whole principle of this old age pension is based, not on the thought that the state is giving something to an indigent or that the state owes something to individuals, but on a sense ' of social justice arising out of a condition of society based1 on the rights of private poverty. While my hon. friend and I may have been fortunate enough to start in life with a little capital and to have had opportunities to make investments that will enable us as we get on to maturer years to look forward to the period between seventy and eighty with a degree of confidence- while that may be possible for him and for me, it is not possible for hundreds of thousands of people in this country, for people working on the farm and in the factory, the people who are day after day producing the
Old Age Pensions

wealth from which we are able to derive our profits, the interest on our investments.
This legislation looks to personality rather than to possessions, it looks to human life rather than to material wealth. We are seeking in making provision for old age to do something which will maintain in the individual that respect and that feeling of pride to which everyone is entitled who serves his day and generation faithfully and well, and serves it against the odds and vicissitudes particularly of our present day. That is the purpose of this legislation, and I am sure that my hon. friend, when he thinks of it from that point of view, will be one of the first to join with the rest of us in doing what he can to have it made part of the law of this land.
May I in conclusion say just one word more? Some hon. members of this House have intimated, indirectly thia afternoon, directly on other occasions, that in this matter the government, and more particularly myself, have been influenced by political considerations; that this legislation is being brought forward not from conviction but for reasons of political expediency. I would ask hon. members to pardon me, in view of that circumstance, if I undertake to give to the House, not words that spring from my lips at the moment, but words which appear in a volume I wrote some years ago and which was published as long ago as eight years. The volume is entitled "Industry and Humanity-Some Principles underlying Industrial Reconstruction." It was alluded to a moment ago by my hon. friend, the member for Calgary. I will read only a paragraph or two, but they will put more succinctly than I am able to do while on my feet at the moment my convictions and beliefs on this matter. In one paragraph dealing with the question of social insurance I have these words:
Social insurance, which in reality is health insurance in one form or another, is a means employed in most industrial countries to bring about a wider measure of social justice, without, on the one hand} disturbing the institution of private property and its advantages to the community, or, on the other, imperilling the thrift and industry of individuals. Social insurance looks upon industry as in the nature of social service. It regards the owner of land or capital as a capitalist, but also as a public trustee. It looks upon the worker in industry as a wage-earner, but equally as a necessary member of the community. It places the emphasis on personality rather than on property, and on life rather than on wealth.
Workmen's compensation, sickness and invalidity insurance, widows' pensions, maternity and infant benefits, recognize wherein personal relationships in industry have changed, and where as a consequence of new conditions permanent handicaps arise. The social legislation of which these measures are an expression rejects, as unworthy, the thought that men and women voluntarily incur accident, sickness, disease, enfeebled health,

or dependence in distress, any more than they willingly seek enslavement of any kind. It recognizes the difficulty of differentiating between industrial accident and occupational disease; and between disease occasioned by occupation or its environments and illness otherwise contracted; also the impossibility of dissociating from economic conditions the social waste caused by excessive and preventable illness. It sees that debt binds health as it binds freedom, that sickness represents the most frequent factor of individual destitution, and that it is in painful crises that handicaps for the whole of life are oftenest imposed. *To save the spirit of men from being crushed is quite as important as to prevent their bodies from being broken or infected. Many a man's spirit fails when, through no fault of his own, or of his family, efficiency is permanently impaired through accident, or savings become exhausted by unemployment or sickness, or where a new life in the home suggests an additional burden instead of a joy. Much invalidity and penury is due to lack of character and thrift; but much also is evidence of want of effective social control. What society fails effectively to prevent, society is in some measure under obligation to mend.
Then coming to old age pensions, I have the following:
Old age pensions are similar. They are based, not on the theory that the state owes every man a living, but rather on the fact that the provision of an assured competence for old age is an easy matter for some, whilst, for others, it is most difficult, if not wholly impossible. After all allowance has been made for superior thrift, intelligence, and integrity, it must be admitted that to the man who has capital to begin with, or whom society permits to own and control vast natural resources, there are opportunities of saving not possible to the worker who possess no capital, and who has to face uncertainties of employment and contend, unaided, against all kinds of vicissitudes. It is obvious that existing forces of world competition operate to rob advanced years of opportunities of employment, which, under the less strenuous regime of earlier times, were available to the close of life. There is need for society to assist in the protection of its members against a condition which simultaneously places burdens upon the worker whose day's work is done, and on the worker whose day's work is just beginning. If the young are to be given a fair start in life, the care of the aged should not be their first responsibility. If life-long public service in industry is to receive its fitting reward, years that are denied opportunity of employment should not be subjected to the humiliation of dependence or charity.
Those words were written, Mr. Speaker, when I had no thought of speaking on this question in the parliament of Canada. I am proud to be able to stand here to-night and to join with others in giving permanent expression in the legislation of our country to the ideas and the purposes that are therein expressed.

Mr. Speaker, I rise not for the purpose of opposing this resolution. As a matter of fact, for some years I have on more than one occasion urged upon parliament the necessity of passing legislation of some character to deal with this problem of caring for old persons who have spent a life in usefulness and service to the community, and I am wholly in accord with the aim of all legis-

Old Age Pensions
lation of this character. The reason I rose a moment ago to ask the hon. the Prime Minister the questions I put was not, as I think he inferred, because I wanted to criticize his position on the matter at all, but rather to clear from my own mind, if possible, the fear that had been lodged there that if this legislation is passed it will not be practicable or effective because of the very fact that we are offering to the provinces a finished product, shall I say, without consultation with them in advance.
I was under the impression, and I still am of that opinion, that this legislation would be more effective, more apt to be applied in a practical manner, if the provinces were consulted beforehand and brought into accord with the objects this parliament has in mind.
As to the suggestions made by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) a moment ago, I must say that there was much in his remarks that impressed me very strongly. However, so far as I am concerned I want to declare my position, and it is simply this:	If the government offers to
parliament this legislation and takes the stand that we must either accept this legislation or none at all I shall find myself forced to vote for it.
I hope that when the bill comes down we may have some more light on the subject. I trust that we shall have in the bill, as no doubt we will, a little more clearly set forth the manner in which the legislation will be applied, and I would hope also that parliament might consider some of the clauses which I shall not take time to go into to-night, and perhaps amend or change some of them so as to make this measure to my mind more practical and more effective. But I wanted to say this, that I stand with many, many others in this House wholly in favour of the very best effort possible being made to solve this, problem of old age pensions, and to assure the government and parliament that the last thing in my mind was to offer obstacles in the way of a solution of the problem. But again I say to the Prime Minister that I do believe the much wiser course would have been to have had a conference with the provinces and come to parliament with a bill which the provinces could have assured us was acceptable to them, or with some assurance that it was a measure a number of the provinces might be willing to accept. For instance, Mr. Speaker, if this measure should be unsuitable to two or three of the major provinces, or only one or two provinces accepted it, that would be a most unhappy outcome. What
we want, if possible, is to get a measure which will be applicable throughout the whole country, suitable and acceptable to all the provinces. That is the point I wish to emphasize ; that is the danger I see at the moment.

I had
no intention whatever of taking any further part in this discussion, in view of the statement I made this afternoon in French that I was thoroughly in accord with the principle of this resolution. But as a military officer, in view of the kind references that have been made to me by the hon. member for Fron-tenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) I feel that I should make a further statement to the House.
Sir, I would have had no objection whatever to the statements the hon. member made tonight if those statements simply referred to myself. But the hon. gentleman has taken it upon himself-and I am not surprised at it, coming from him-to make the statements he did at a time when two prominent men in this House, the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn) and the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) two former ministers under whom I served, were absent, from the chamber. Had these hon. gentlemen been present they could have furnished to the House a thorough explanation of the reasons why I was compelled to take my pension in 1922, and their explanation would have given a different aspect to the matter from that which the hon. member for Frontenae-Addington placed upon it.
The statement the hon. member has made that I am drawing a pension at the present time as an officer of the permanent force serving at headquarters is not absolutely correct. Bearing in mind the despatches that were read in the old House of Commons after the battle of Paardeberg, and remembering the decorations I received for my services in South Africa, I can easily say that I am not ashamed of my services at that time. I was quite willing to perform the same services in 1914, but I was refused the necessary permission, notwithstanding the fact that I offered to resign my rank and serve as a Lieutenant-Colonel in the ambulance corps. I was one of the first to volunteer for service overseas, but I was told by the minister at the head of the department at the time, and also by the then Prime Minister of this country, that my place was here and that my duty lay in Canada.
Did I question that?

You did.

Further than that, I was forced to retire from the service in 1922. I did not go voluntarily; I was compelled to retire after undergoing a surgical operation of the most serious character-a fact which the hon. member for East Hamilton could easily have vouched for. I was forced to take my pension and go and live in the country. For a year, Sir, I was there on sick leave, having hemorrhages every fifteen days, and suffering to such an extent that in April, 1923, I had to go under the knife for the second time. During that period I applied to the government to extend my leave of absence, and the only answer I received when I was on the hospital bed was that my successor had been appointed. Therefore, Sir, the pension I am drawing was awarded because I was not in a fit state of health to perform my duties.
There is another point that has been forgotten, and it is this: no man in this country has paid as much for the pension he is enjoying as I have paid. Towards that pension I contributed five per cent of my salary during a period of thirty years of service. There is not a judge in the country, there is not a brother officer of the permanent corps, who has made contributions to the pension fund to the same extent. I paid that five per cent not only on my full salary as deputy minister, but also on my salary as vice president of the militia council.
I apologize, Mr. Speaker, for taking the time of the House to make these remarks but I consider that no hon. member has a right to make such glaring statements as those which have been made with respect to me tonight. I only wish I could characterize that conduct in language that is parliamentary. The reason for my speaking the second time is that I wanted to offer a defence, to the best of my ability in respect to the insinuations directed to-night against those men who were compelled to remain at headquarters here during the whole duration of the war and who performed loyally, and to the best of their ability, as I have done myself, Sir, their duty to their common country and to the empire.

Mr. Speaker, I am not quite sure whether I have the right to rise to a question of privilege. I merely want to assure the hon. gentleman that I cast no imputation on his loyalty or on his courage in any degree-none whatever. I say now, as I said before,, that the hon. member is drawing a pension which has been given to him and

to others. I also say that viewing the matter of pensions as I do I only wish I had the power to wipe the system off the statute books and prevent him and many others from receiving them.
